passages.text: An Equine Protein Atlas Highlights Synovial Fluid Proteome Dynamics during Experimentally LPS-Induced Arthritis

In human proteomics, substantial efforts are ongoing to leverage large collections of mass spectrometry (MS) fragment ion spectra into extensive spectral libraries (SL) as a resource for data independent acquisition (DIA) analysis. Currently, such initiatives in equine research are still missing. Here we present a large-scale equine SL, comprising 6394 canonical proteins and 89,329 unique peptides, based on data dependent acquisition analysis of 75 tissue and body fluid samples from horses. The SL enabled large-scale DIA-MS based quantification of the same samples to generate a quantitative equine protein distribution atlas to infer dominant proteins in different organs and body fluids. Data mining revealed 163 proteins uniquely identified in a specific type of tissue or body fluid, serving as a starting point to determine tissue-specific or tissue-type-specific proteins. We showcase the SL by highlighting proteome dynamics in equine synovial fluid samples during experimental lipopolysaccharide-induced arthritis. A fuzzy c-means cluster analysis pinpointed SERPINB1, ATRN, NGAL, LTF, MMP1, and LBP as putative biomarkers for joint inflammation. This SL provides an extendable resource for future equine studies employing DIA-MS.
Introduction

In mass spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics, data independent acquisition (DIA) has developed into a compelling alternative to data dependent acquisition (DDA) for identification and quantification of proteins and peptides in complex biological samples. In DIA, the mass spectrometer cycles over user-defined isolation windows to analyze all precursor ions across the liquid chromatography (LC) gradient. In this way, DIA overcomes the stochastic nature of the traditional DDA approach, where precursor ions are selected for analysis based on abundance, leading to a more complete and reliable coverage of the proteome. Following data acquisition, peptide and protein identifications are extracted via targeted data analysis, using a reference spectral library (SL) containing annotated sets of spectra required for protein identification. The SL is usually generated from previously acquired DDA and DIA-MS data to establish a nonredundant, curated, and searchable compendium of spectra. An alternative analysis strategy is the library-free approach, but this has in some instances been shown to be less sensitive than the SL-based strategy. It is consequently of significant importance to construct SLs with high proteome coverage while maintaining strict control of the false discovery rate (FDR) to reach the highest possible depth and quantification accuracy in DIA. In the proteomics research community, billions of fragment ions are acquired during MS studies. To advance the field in human research, initiatives have been formed with the aim to leverage these data sets into a SL resource for the processing of all new DIA data acquired. Currently, there is still no such initiative in equine research, but the use of SLs are emerging.-

In recent years, the horse has been increasingly used as an animal model for various diseases including osteoarthritis (OA), atrial fibrillation, and infectious and allergic diseases, where size, physiology, anatomy, and other aspects confer specific validity to the equine model. The increasing traction of research involving horses engender a growing demand for technologies such as MS-based proteomics, since validated heterologous antibodies for immunoassays are a scarce resource and there has been limited financial incentive to raise equine-specific antibodies. As an alternative strategy, MS-based proteomics has been successfully adopted to quantify, e.g., acute phase proteins in wound healing, septic articular pathologies, the peritoneal fluid composition following intestinal strangulation, and the abundance of proteins in saliva in response to systemic inflammation. Besides being a good model for joint diseases in humans, the equine joint is a compartment undergoing intensive investigation as equine joint diseases is one of the major causes of equine morbidity and poor welfare. Essential insight into the pathology of equine joint diseases, e.g., osteoarthritis and septic arthritis, has been obtained using proteomics, but further proteomics studies are required. Early diagnosis of joint pathology is of particular importance for early intervention, and the initial pathology of joint inflammation can be studied by the use of an equine experimental model of lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced arthritis.-

In contrast to collective efforts in other animal model systems, the absence of large-scale cataloging of the equine organ proteome landscape has precluded the construction of a high-quality SL that could serve as a starting point to further advance targeted proteomics (SRM/PRM/MRM) and DIA approaches in the horse. Another shortage in equine proteome research is the poor annotation of the genome and proteome. Of the 44,484 Uniprot entries, only 291 proteins are reviewed (Uniprot entry 2023-03-06), and it is unknown which proteins are expressed and how proteins distribute across tissues and body fluids. Extensive SLs exist for both human and mouse, and besides providing the foundation for publicly available SLs, these efforts have catalyzed large-scale protein abundance and protein distribution analysis in health and disease.

Here we present an equine SL based on DDA analysis of 15 different tissues and four body fluids from the horse. Based on DIA-MS protein abundance profiles across the different types of samples, we constructed a protein distribution map of the horse proteome that can be used to infer dominant proteins in different organs and body compartments. We showcase the resource by analyzing proteome dynamics in synovial fluid (SF) samples sequentially during experimental LPS-induced arthritis, with the purpose of obtaining new insights into LPS-induced joint inflammation.
Experimental Section
Study Design and Analysis Rationale

In this study, we used DDA-MS to profile the proteome of 75 samples from 15 different tissue types and four body fluids obtained from 12 individual horses and used the data to generate an SL. The tissue and body fluid samples were collected in at least three healthy biological replicates, except for synovial membrane (one replicate), to measure the biological variation. The horses were considered healthy based on clinical assessment and routine blood analyses obtained before euthanasia, and for joint tissue and SF an additional macroscopic inspection of the joint cavity was performed post mortem. Inflammation is a cardinal symptom in many diseases, leading to substantial reorganization of the tissue and cellular proteomes. To increase the coverage of the SL, we included tissue and fluid samples representing an inflammatory state, both acute (strangulated jejunum, periphlebitis, and SF from joints with LPS-induced arthritis) and chronic (SF and tissue from joints with OA and tissue from a limb wound 14 days post wounding). Next, samples were analyzed in DIA-MS mode, and the SL was used to generate a quantitative equine protein distribution atlas.

To showcase the developed SL, SF samples from three horses with highly inflammatory LPS-induced experimental arthritis were sequentially sampled at five different time points (0, 1, 16, 24, and 48 h) and evaluated with DIA analysis and processed with the SL as the reference library. A fuzzy c-means cluster analysis (clustering method where every data point is assigned a cluster and a probability of it being in the cluster) was used to get insight into the clustering of the quantified proteins based on the protein dynamics.
Samples
Samples Included in the SL

Seventy-five samples from 12 horses representing 15 different tissues and four different body fluids were included. They are termed the "Tissue-Fluid samples". The types of samples were specifically selected to cover the major vascularized organs (liver, spleen, kidney, and lymph nodes), the internal organs most often involved in morbidity in horses: digestive system (jejunum, cecum, and colon), joint compartment (synovial membrane, cartilage, and subchondral bone), respiratory system (lung), ubiquitous tissues (adipose tissue and muscle), and the body fluids most commonly used for diagnostics (serum, plasma, SF, and peritoneal fluid). The Tissue-Fluid samples were isolated from healthy horses along with additional specific samples from horses with local inflammatory condition. The horses were Standardbred trotters and Cobs, mares, and geldings, 3-14 years old. Supplementary File 1 provides an overview of the samples included in the protein atlas.

Specific samples were obtained with permission from the Danish Animal Experiments Inspectorate (License 2017-15-0201-01314 (horse IDs H5, H9, H10, H11, and H12) and 2011/561-1996 (horse IDs H8 and SF used to validate the SL)). Samples from horse IDs H6 and H7 were leftover SF after synoviocenteses from client-owned horses, stored for research purposes with the owners' consent. The remaining samples were obtained from euthanized research horses (horse IDs H1, H2, H3, and H4) from unrelated terminal studies. All sampling procedures were approved by the ethics and welfare committee of the Department of Veterinary Clinical Sciences, University of Copenhagen, and procedures were carried out according to the Danish Act on animal experiments.

Samples with horse IDs H5, H9, H10, H11, and H12 originated from an experimental equine OA model described in previous studies. In short, OA was induced by creating an 8 mm osteochondral fragment on the radial carpal bone under arthroscopic guidance. From day 14 and until euthanasia at day 71, horses underwent exercise on a treadmill 5 days/week. The contralateral joint underwent sham surgery and was sampled similarly to the operated joint, thus serving as a healthy control. SF was sampled regularly over the study period from both OA and healthy control joints.
Synovial Fluid Samples from Horses with Experimental LPS-Induced Arthritis (LPS-SF)

The SF used to validate the SL (and the Tissue-Fluid samples with horse ID H8) originated from a study aimed at characterizing intra-articular hemostatic and inflammatory responses in experimental LPS-induced acute arthritis as described in detail previously. In short, acute arthritis was induced by intra-articular injection of LPS in one antebrachiocarpal joint. SF was aspirated aseptically from the joint at regular intervals over the next 24 h and transferred to citrate-coated tubes. The study included determination of the concentration of the inflammatory acute phase proteins serum amyloid A (SAA), fibrinogen (FIB), and haptoglobin (HP) in the SF samples using commercial assays.
Sample Processing

All Tissue-Fluid samples obtained post mortem were sampled within 5 h after euthanasia. Tissue samples were immediately washed in PBS to remove blood/SF, snap frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at -80  C until analysis. All tissue samples were digested within 4 months from sampling.

To ensure that the SL covered a broad spectrum of proteins and embracing proteins potentially favored by various preparation steps, several different processing methods were used for body fluids. Blood was collected in tubes with clot activator (serum) or EDTA-coated tubes (plasma), peritoneal fluid in EDTA-coated tubes, and SF in plain tubes, EDTA-coated tubes, or citrate-coated tubes, all based on the initial purpose for which the sample was obtained. Protease inhibitor (cOmplete Protease Inhibitor Cocktail, Roche) (25x) was added to a number of plasma, peritoneal fluid, and SF samples (Supplementary File 1). Blood samples in tubes with a clot activator were centrifuged at 1800 g for 10 min at RT after a clot was established. Blood and SF samples in EDTA coated tubes were centrifuged at 1000 g for 20 min at 4  C. SF samples in citrate-coated tubes were centrifuged at 1500 g for 15 min at RT, and SF in plain tubes were centrifuged at 2500 g for 10 min at 4  C. Two plasma samples and three SF samples (Supplementary File 1) were enriched for lower abundant proteins by the use of ProteoMiner (large capacity kit) according to the manufacturer's protocol , followed by buffer exchange (2.5 M GuHcl, 250 mM HEPES, pH 7.8) in a 3 kDa cut off spin filter (Merck Millipore). All body fluid samples were digested within 6 months upon sampling except SF in plain tubes (digested within a year from sampling) and SF in citrate-coated tubes (digested after ~3 years from sampling).
The LPS-SF were sampled in citrate-coated tubes and processed as already described for the SF samples in citrate-coated tubes. The samples were digested ~3 years from sampling.
Digest and Desalting

Tissue-Fluid samples and LPS-SF samples ((6-8) x 1 mm3 cubes of each tissue, fluids ~100 mug protein) were dissolved in 8 M urea (Sigma-Aldrich) in 100 mM ammonium bicarbonate and processed by ultrasonication (Bioruptor Pico, Diagenode) for 10 min at 4  C, 20 cycles, 15 s ON and 15 s OFF. Protein disulfide bonds were reduced with 5 mM Tris(2-carboxyethyl) phosphine (Sigma-Aldrich) for 60 min at 37  C and alkylated with 10 mM iodoacetamide for 30 min at RT in the dark, followed by addition of 100 mM ammonium bicarbonate to a final urea concentration below 1.5 M. Proteins were digested with trypsin (min. 1:100 w/w) at 37  C for an hour followed by another addition of trypsin (min. 1:100 w/w) and digestion overnight at 37  C. The digestion was quenched by the addition of 10% formic acid to pH   3. The samples were centrifuged for 10 min at 14,000 g and the supernatant was desalted using the Thermo Scientific SOLAmu vacuum manifold and solid phase extraction micro elution as follows: The columns were conditioned with 200 muL acetonitrile, equilibrated with 400 muL 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid, and 250 muL of the sample was loaded and diluted in 250 muL 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid. The sample on the column was washed with 500 muL of 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid then 200 muL of 0.1% formic acid and eluted with 50 muL of 50% acetonitrile and 0.2% formic acid two times. The samples were vacuum-dried and resuspended in 50 muL of HPLC water with 2% acetonitrile, 0.2% formic acid, and synthetic peptides (1:20 v/v) (iRT peptide kit, Biognosys AG) for retention time calibration. The peptide concentration was measured by use of the Pierce Quantitative Colorimetric Peptide Assay (Thermo Scientific) according to the manufacturer's protocol .
MS Analysis

Samples were separated on a PepMap RSLC C18 analytical column (75 mum x 50 cm, 2 mum, 100 A, nanoViper, Thermo Scientific) using the EASY-nanoLC system (Thermo Scientific) coupled to a Q Exactive HF-X Hybrid Quadropole-Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific). Separation of 1 mug of peptide mixture was achieved by running a constant flow rate of 350 nL/min in 0.1% formic acid/99.9% water and a 120 min gradient from 10% to 90% (10% for 90 min, 30% for 20 min, 45% for 1 min, and 90% for 10 min) elution buffer (80% acetonitrile, 0.1% formic acid, and 19.9% water) (Supplementary File 2).

For DDA analysis, Xcalibur 4.1.31.9 June 2017 was applied to record the spectra. The full scan MS spectra (350-1400 m/z) were acquired with a resolution of 60,000 after accumulation to a target value of 3e6. Higher-energy collisional-induced dissociation MS/MS spectra with fixed first mass of 100 m/z were recorded from the 15 most intense signals with a resolution of 15,000 applying an automatic gain control of 1e5 and a maximum injection time of 60 ms. Precursors were isolated using a window of 1.3 m/z and fragmented with a normalized collision energy of 28%. The intensity threshold for precursor ion selection was 1.7e4. Precursor ions with an unassigned or single charge state were rejected, and precursor masses already selected for MS/MS were excluded for further selection for 10 s. DDA data for Tissue-Fluid samples were acquired in two different batches. Blanks were included after every fourth sample.

For DIA, the full scan MS spectra (340-1410 m/z) were acquired with a resolution of 60,000 after accumulation to a target value of 3e6 and a maximum injection time of 100 ms. The MS/MS data was recorded by 32 full fragmentation scans, using an isolation window adjusted to the number of peaks (Supplementary File 2). The precursor ions within each isolation window were fragmented using higher-energy collisional-induced dissociation with a resolution of 30,000 applying an automatic gain control of 1e6 and a maximum injection time of 120 ms. DIA data for Tissue-Fluid samples were acquired in two different batches. Blanks were included after every fourth sample.
Data Analysis
Building the Spectral Library

DDA files from the 75 Tissue-Fluid samples were compiled into an SL using the pulsar search engine in the commercial software Spectronaut v. 16.2.220903.53000 on an Equus caballus reference proteome FASTA database with reviewed and unreviewed (TrEMBL) proteins from Uniprot release 22_05, totaling 44,484 entries using default Biognosys (BGS) factory settings. Trypsin (P) was specified as the enzyme with up to two missed cleavages, allowing a minimum of five and maximum of 50 amino acids and including proteins identified with only one peptide to present the global proteome. Mass tolerance intervals for fragment ions were set to 200-3000 m/z.
Searching DIA Data

A database search of the 75 DIA files from the Tissue-Fluid samples was carried out in Spectronaut, using the previously built SL as a search database in library mode. The search was configured using the default BGS factory settings with FDR set to 0.01 at both the peptide and protein level. The DIA files from the SF samples from the LPS study were searched using the same library and configuration settings as above.
Protein Quantification

For the DIA search result of the Tissue-Fluid samples, the peptides were inferred to protein quantities using the Spectronaut built-in maxLFQ algorithm. For the LPS-SF, the DIA search result file was processed using the software MapDIA v.3.1.0 inferring peptides to protein quantities given that the peptides are unique to the protein, with a minimum of one unique peptide per inferred protein.
Imputation

Protein quantification data sets from Tissue-Fluid samples and LPS-SF samples contained cases where proteins were quantified in some of the samples, and the other part resulted in NA values due to insufficient quantifiable peptides. The assumption is that the samples with NA values are manifestations of a very low concentration or total absence of the protein and therefore not detected in the MS. To simulate this, every sample with a protein NA value was imputed by a random draw from a uniform distribution ranging from 5% to 50% of the minimum observed quantified value of the protein.

In eq 1, the imputed sample protein value (ISPv) is obtained by a random draw from a uniform distribution (U) based on a range of 0.05 to 0.5 times the minimum observed quantified protein value (OQPvmin). For the calculation of the CV, missing values were not imputed but proteins with missing values in one or more samples were simply left out.
Normalization

For global comparison of DIA-SL samples, a VSN strategy was used to bring the quantitative data from heterogeneous samples onto a same scale, making the sample variance nondependent from the mean intensity. The LPS-SF data were median normalized and log 2 transformed. Median normalization was also applied for the calculation of CVs.
Analysis of the SF Data from Horses with Experimental LPS-Induced Arthritis

Only proteins identified with at least two unique peptides and identified in at least five samples were included in the analysis, and the mean intensity signal per time point was used in the fuzzy c-means cluster analysis. The number of clusters was set to four, based on the point of inflection when imaging the within cluster sum of squared error and a correlation between clusters below 0.75. Only proteins with a membership score >0.5 were considered true members of the designated cluster. Median-normalized and nonimputed data from analysis of DIA-SL tissue samples from healthy individuals were used to uncover the potential tissue origin of proteins identified in LPS-SF. The protein abundance in the different tissues was scaled to the sum of all the abundances for the protein.

R (v. 4.1.2) was used for imputation, normalization, and analysis. Metascape was used for enrichment analysis of GO biological processes with min overlap at five and min enrichment at two. Protein intersection analysis was performed using Venny v. 2.1 and UpSet. Additional graphics were created in GraphPad Prism v. 9.3.0, Adobe Illustrator and BioRender. The MS data has been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE partner repository with the data set identifier PXD044741 and is publicly available.
Results and Discussion
Protein Profiling Across Tissues and Body Fluids

The equine SL was generated by combining data from 75 nonfractionated samples from 19 different tissues and body fluids originating from 12 different healthy and diseased horses. All tissue samples were processed for MS analysis and analyzed in DDA-MS mode and the resulting data used to generate an SL encompassing 6394 unique proteins and 89,329 peptides. Only 291 proteins of the 44,484 entries in the Uniprot equine proteome database were marked as reviewed, and 181 of these proteins were identified in the equine SL presented here. This means that the equine SL provided evidence for 6213 unreviewed proteins (14%) in the equine proteome in Uniprot (more details on protein and peptide identification can be found in Supplementary File 3).

This is the most extensive equine SL presented to date, and our hope is that the comprehensive data set presented here provides a valuable resource for future equine studies employing the DIA-MS approach and may act as a general and publicly available equine SL that can be further expanded in the future. Development of project-specific SLs requires a considerable investment of time in sample preparation and analysis, but with large community-shared SLs as presented here, a common set of reference spectra ready to apply is provided, often resulting in higher protein coverage compared to project-specific SLs. Such extensive libraries are required to quantitatively compare heterogeneous samples in larger-sized cohorts such as clinical studies.

In the next step, all samples were analyzed using DIA and the SL was used to infer dominant proteins in the different organs and body compartments by targeted data extraction to generate a quantitative equine protein distribution atlas. In total, this analysis generated quantitative protein profiles for 5934 canonical proteins and 83,728 unique peptides. The average number of proteins was 3123 for tissue samples and 448 for body fluids (Supplementary File 1).

A Pearson correlation of the median normalized log transformed protein abundances was used to compare the correlation between the biological replicates within the sample type and condition. The correlation coefficients were between 0.67 and 0.95 for tissue and 0.76 and 0.97 for body fluids (Figure 1). The distribution profiles obtained with the Pearson correlation analysis revealed three major distinct groups: one group with body fluids, a group with cartilage and subchondral bone, and a group encompassing the rest of the tissues included in the correlation analysis, where the correlation was more diverse. Some samples had a negative correlation, which was caused by proteins with high abundance in one tissue/body fluid and low abundance in another tissue/body fluid (Supplementary File 4).

Pearson correlation of the median normalized log transformed protein abundances for samples with more than one biological replicate. Only proteins identified in all samples of the same type were included in the correlation analysis. Red boxes indicate three major distinct groups. H, horse; SF, synovial fluid; PI, protease inhibitor; PM, proteoMiner; OA, osteoarthritis; C, control; D, day. Graphics created with RStudio (corrplot, RColorBrewer).

To compare the protein abundances observed in all 75 samples, raw imputed DIA data was VSN normalized and visualized in a heatmap with clustering (Figure 2). The heatmap column dendogram showed two overall clusters: a cluster with all body fluids, inflamed jejunum, subchondral bone, and all but two cartilage samples and a second cluster with the remaining tissue samples. Gene ontology analysis of clusters of proteins with high abundance revealed the enrichment of specific biological processes. Proteins with high abundance in muscle mapped to Generation of precursor metabolites and energy, Oxidative phosphorylation, and Muscle system process, proteins with high abundance in body fluids mapped to Humoral immune response, Negative regulation of blood coagulation, and Negative regulation of hydrolase activity, and proteins with high abundance in cartilage and subchondral bone mapped to Skeletal system development. Proteins with high abundance in samples from the intestine mapped to Actin cytoskeleton organization, Muscle structure development, and Actin-filament-based processes.

Heatmap shows the VSN normalized protein abundances and the hierarchical clustering of the proteins. The arrows point out protein clusters (marked in dashed red) with high abundance and combine with the enriched biological processes for those proteins based on gene ontology (GO) analysis. The GO analysis shows that proteins with high abundance levels in distinct samples mapped to familiar biological processes for the given organ. H, horse; SF, synovial fluid; PI, protease inhibitor; PM, proteoMiner; OA, osteoarthritis; C, control; D, day; Inf, inflammation (periphlebitis); Strang, strangulated. Graphics created with RStudio (heatmap.2), Adobe Illustrator, and BioRender.

In conclusion, we identified and quantified the proteome from 15 different tissue types and four body fluids obtained from 12 individual horses. The results provided evidence for 14% of the unreviewed uniprot entries and was used to generate the most extensive equine SL to date. The proteomes from biological replicates of the same sample type and condition showed a high degree of correlation, and the proteins with high abundance levels in distinct samples mapped to familiar biological processes for the given organ.
Protein Distribution and Dynamics of the Equine Protein Tissue Atlas

Measuring the protein dynamics in tissues and body fluids is fundamental to understanding biology and disease mechanisms. Mining of the equine protein distribution atlas generated new insights into the protein distribution in different tissues, fluids, and body compartments and enabled the identification of tissue-specific proteins of potential relevance when studying different disease mechanisms. Figure 3 shows how the protein distribution in different types of samples (excluding wound and inflamed vein) intersected. Interestingly, 163 proteins were only identified in one specific type of tissue or body fluid, serving as a starting point to determine tissue-specific or tissue-type-specific proteins (Supplementary File 5). As examples observed in both the DDA and DIA data set, three Paneth-cell-specific alpha-defensins (DEFA) not detected in other mammalian species, e.g., cattle, pig, or dog, were uniquely identified in equine jejunum. They have been shown to be important in the defense mechanism of the small bowel mucosa toward prominent human and equine pathogens such as Staphylococcus aureus, Salmonella typhimurium, and Escherichia coli. Their presence and tissue specificity make the horse an obvious species to study biological properties of alpha-defensins. Uromodulin (UMOD), dendrin (DDN), and 12 solute carrier family (SLC) members were identified only in the kidney tissue samples. They are known to be kidney-specific proteins and to be of major physiological importance in humans but are also involved in various kidney disorders. These have not previously been investigated in horses. Furthermore, SLC22A6, a transporter of drugs, is believed to facilitate interorgan communication around the gut-liver-kidney axis, and studies involving SLC22A6 have the potential to provide knowledge about altered drug disposition pathways in different organs in kidney diseases. Other examples of tissue-specific proteins were solute carrier organic anion transporter family member (SLCO1B3), tyrosine aminotransferase (TAT), and bile salt export pump (ABCB11), all three of which were exclusively identified in liver samples and pulmonary surfactant-associated protein C (SFTPC) unique to samples from the lung. Various proteins involved in striated muscle contraction and muscle system processes were exclusively identified in muscle. In lymph nodes, the protein linker for activation of T-cell family member (LAT) 1, LAT2, and signaling lymphocytic activation molecule family member 1 (SLAMF1) were uniquely identified. Investigation of such tissue-specific proteins in both health and disease might reveal tissue-specific events of relevance for both horses and humans.

Articular joints constitute a semiclosed environment, which is subject to intense investigation in many diseases, e.g., OA. To understand the pathogenesis of joint diseases and to develop disease-specific diagnostics and therapeutics, it is important to have an insight into the tissue of origin of identified proteins. Both SF, synovial membrane, cartilage, and subchondral bone samples were included here, and Figure 4A shows the relationship of the identified proteins in the DIA data in the different sample types.

(A) Venn diagram showing the relation between the global proteomes identified in cartilage, subchondral bone, synovial membrane, and synovial fluid. (B) List of intersecting proteins identified in cartilage (CAR), subchondral bone (SB), and synovial fluid (SF), but not synovial membrane samples, involved in skeletal system development, extracellular matrix organization, and ossification. Graphics created with Venny.

The proteins exclusively identified in the synovial membrane and cartilage were related to intracellular processes. Some cartilage matrix proteins have been investigated in OA, but little information is available regarding the disturbances in subchondral bone. In accordance with a recently published study, osteocalcin (BGLAP), Indian hedgehog (IHH), and calsyntenin 1 (CTNNBIP1) were only identified in subchondral bone both in the DDA and the DIA data sets and the tissue specificity of these proteins might be of particular interest when studying pathological events in joint diseases. Research in joint diseases often focuses on identification of biomarkers in SF reflecting pathological events in the osteochondral unit. Figure 4B shows a list of intersecting proteins involved in skeletal system development and ossification identified in SF and in cartilage and/or subchondral bone but not in synovial membrane samples. These proteins could be potential biomarkers for degradation of tissues in the osteochondral unit, which may be of interest for biomarker studies in the joint disease research community. Cellular communication factor 3 (CCN3) was identified in subchondral bone, cartilage, and SF. In a previous study it has been shown that, after completion of endochondral ossification, CCN3 was observed in few cell types in bone marrow, with expression being dramatically enhanced after bone injury. Intra-articular administration of CCN3 has been reported to have a favorable treatment effect in murine OA models, but it has recently been found to enhance cartilage degeneration when used for longer periods. Its potential as a biomarker and therapeutic target is still under investigation, and OA research in horse models might contribute to establishing evidence. Chordin-like protein 2 (CHRDL2) was identified in cartilage and SF and has previously been found to be downregulated on the gene level in cartilage from joints with OA and suggested as a biomarker for this condition. In conclusion, the SL confers knowledge about specific proteins that might be central in specific joint pathologies or potential biomarkers of interest for the research community within joint diseases.
Synovial Fluid from Experimental LPS Arthritis Study

Diagnosis and monitoring of septic arthritis can be challenging, and early diagnosis is crucial for a successful outcome. Insight into the protein dynamics during the initial hours of disease progression can give important knowledge about the disease pathology and identify a panel of potential biomarkers for early diagnosis. To demonstrate that the SL can facilitate the identification of putative biomarker candidates, we applied the SL as a database to search DIA data from analysis of SF sequentially sampled during the initial hours of experimental LPS-induced arthritis, a model of septic arthritis, in three horses. Time dependent DIA-MS analysis using the established SL demonstrated that dynamic changes of SAA1, FIB, and HP (Figure 5) were in line with a previous analysis of the same samples using commercial assays. Currently, global analysis of the dynamic changes in protein expression during inflammatory arthritis in horses has only been scarcely investigated, and the SL is thus expected to significantly advance this research topic.

Time-resolved dynamics of the proteins serum amyloid A1 (SAA1) (Uniprot accession number in parentheses), fibrinogen A, fibrinogen B, and haptoglobin in synovial fluid from three horses (H1, H2, and H3) with LPS-induced experimental arthritis from 0 h (before intra-articular LPS injection) to 48 h post injection. Graphics created with GraphPad Prism.

We used fuzzy c-means cluster analysis of the protein expression profiles to study the SF proteome dynamics during LPS-induced acute arthritis in more detail. Based on the time-resolved protein fluctuations, most of the identified proteins could be divided into four distinct clusters (Figure 6 and Supplementary File 6).

Fuzzy c-means cluster analysis of the protein expression profiles in synovial fluid during the initial 48 h of LPS-induced experimental arthritis in three horses. Only proteins identified with at least two peptides and identified in at least five samples were included in the analysis. The protein abundances were log transformed and missing values were imputed based on the assumption of missing not a random. The mean of the protein abundance per time point (T) was used in the analysis. For each cluster, the enriched GO biological processes with the highest q-value is shown. T1, 0 h; T2, 8 h; T3, 16 h; T4, 24 h; T5, 48 h; Pos., positive; Reg., regulation. Graphics created with RStudio (tidyverse).

The proteins in cluster 1 showed a marked increase in abundance toward 8 h followed by a steady level toward 48 h. The most enriched biological processes were Regulation of cell substrate adhesion, Actin filament organization, Inflammatory response, and Positive regulation of cell adhesion. Proteins with a prompt and marked change in abundance, such as the proteins mapping to cluster 1, are of relevance as early disease biomarkers. The cluster included SERPINB1, which has previously been shown to have an important role in the resolution of inflammatory diseases and in the host response to some infections, attractin (ATRN), which is involved in immune cell clustering in the initial phases of inflammation, and l-selectin (SELL), essential for lymphocyte homing and leukocyte trafficking. Also, inter-alpha-trypsin inhibitor 1 (ITIH1), ITIH2, ITIH3, and ITIH4 and lipocalin 2 (LCN2), also called neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL), mapped to cluster 1. Using an ELISA validated for equine samples, two recent studies have investigated the biomarker potential of NGAL in equine inflammatory arthritis. One study evaluated NGAL in clinical cases with septic arthritis and found nearly perfect discriminatory ability. In another study evaluating NGAL in horses with LPS-induced arthritis, concentrations increased within a few hours of LPS injection and peaked between 6 and 9 h, thus confirming that NGAL is an early marker of inflammatory arthritis in horses. The acute phase proteins SAA1, FIB, and HP also mapped to cluster 1.

The cluster 2 proteins showed a prompt increase in abundance toward 8 h followed by a decrease to an abundance above the starting point at 48 h. The most enriched biological processes were Humoral immune response, Blood coagulation, Actin-filament-based processes, and Regulation of defense response. This cluster included the cytokine interleukin (IL)-6, a potent inducer of the acute phase response, which was expected, but this low-abundant protein was only identified in eight of the 15 samples. In addition, neutrophil elastase (ELANE) secreted by neutrophils during inflammation, lactotransferrin (LTF), matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) 8, and tissue inhibitor of MMP (TIMP1) mapped to cluster 2. Lactotransferrin (LTF) has previously been identified in higher concentration compared to the control in SF in clinical cases of septic arthritis in the horse and might be considered as a diagnostic or prognostic biomarker (Figure 6).

Proteins in cluster 3 decreased markedly in abundance toward 16 h followed by an increase in abundance toward the 48 h but never reached the initial level. Ossification, Regulation of insulin-like growth factor receptor signaling pathway, Extracellular matrix organization, and Skeletal system development were the most enriched biological processes. The proteins mapping to extracellular matrix organization included fibulin 1 (FBLN1), fibromodulin (FMOD), lumican (LUM), MMP9, cartilage oligomeric matrix protein (COMP), and transforming growth factor beta-induced protein (TGFBI). These proteins are likely involved in or are a product of cartilage degradation triggered by LPS as previously shown in in vitro studies on human chondrocytes.

The abundance of proteins in cluster 4 showed a steady increase over time. Negative regulation of proteolysis, Acute phase response, Positive regulation of cytokine production, and Regulation of cellular response to growth factor stimulus were the most enriched biological processes and included an extrahepatic isoform of serum amyloid A (SAA2), lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA) and LDHB, lipopolysaccharide-binding protein (LBP), and MMP1, MMP2, and MMP19 known to degrade components of the cartilage extracellular matrix in arthritic disease.- Nine members of the SERPIN family also mapped to cluster 4; SERPINA3 (chymotrypsin), SERPINA6 (hormone binding), SERPINA7 (antitrypsin-like), SERPINA10 (inhibitor of activated coagulation factor Z and XI), SERPINB10 (inhibitory protein involved in hematopoietic and myeloid development), SERPINC1 (antithrombin III), SERPIND1 (thrombin inhibitor), SERPINF2 (involved in fibrinolysis), and SERPING1 (C1 inhibitor). Even with their slower increase in abundance, proteins in cluster 4 could also be of value for diagnosis of joint disease.

A protein that might be of interest in septic arthritis caused by Gram-negative bacteria is the protein LBP (Figure 6). LBP is an LPS receptor and the LPS-LBP complex interacts with CD14 and triggers monocyte secretion of cytokines. This interaction could also be a therapeutic target, because LPS binding of the bactericidal permeability increasing protein (BPI) hinders the binding of LBP and antagonizes the proinflammatory effect of LBP. A therapeutic agent with the capacity to block LBP binding could potentially mitigate the inflammatory response.

Based on the change in concentration and/or known relation to the inflammatory response, as well as the consistency of quantification at most of the time points, the findings in the present study support SERPINB1, ATRN, NGAL, LTF, MMP1, and LBP as putative biomarkers for joint inflammation (Figure 7).

Time-resolved dynamics of putative markers for joint inflammation. The protein abundance observed for each horse (H1, H2, and H3) and the standard deviations are included. Data are the log transformed imputed data. Imputed data points are marked with no fill in the point shape. T1, 0 h; T2, 8 h; T3, 16 h; T4, 24 h; and T5, 48 h after LPS-induced experimental arthritis. Graphics created with GraphPad Prism.

The equine septic arthritis proteome has been studied in a few previous studies. In one study, the time-resolved changes in protein composition focusing on potential biomarkers of eradication of infection was analyzed using label-free DDA-MS. Arthritis was experimentally induced in horses by intra-articular injection of either very low amounts of LPS or a clinical strain of E. coli, and it was shown that SF levels of the sensitive inflammatory biomarker SAA increased in response to bacterial infection and peaked at day 4, which corresponds to how naturally occurring septic arthritis evolves in horses. High concentrations of SAA determined by immunoassays has been demonstrated in several studies on equine septic arthritis. In another study, the SF proteome of horses with clinical septic arthritis was characterized by the use of MS but with no time-resolved observations, and similar to our results, LTF was identified to be a potentially useful biomarker in equine arthritis.

The SF proteome is maintained by influx and efflux of proteins from the surrounding tissues, and it is known that the permeability of the synovial membrane increases markedly in response to septic arthritis and results in a more systemic inflammatory response affecting many organs in the body. But a detailed understanding of the factors behind the control of the SF proteome in health and disease is still missing. Previously, the dynamics in the blood plasma proteome were investigated in mice, which unraveled the extent to which various tissues contributed to alterations in plasma protein composition in sepsis. We used the protein-organ distribution atlas generated here to unravel the potential tissue distribution of proteins identified in SF from joints with LPS-induced arthritis, which is important information to strengthen our knowledge of the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms. Another benefit of knowing the protein origin is that tissue-specific biomarkers can be of great value. The role and involvement of subchondral bone in joint pathology is becoming increasingly recognized, and specific biomarkers from cartilage and subchondral bone are important to better understand the pathophysiology of joint tissue degeneration and staging joint pathology. Several proteins identified in SF from joints with LPS-induced arthritis were also predominantly identified in healthy cartilage and/or subchondral bone samples, thus suggesting these tissues as the potential origin of the protein (Supplementary File 7). As an example, matrix Gla protein (MGP) was found in SF from horses with LPS-induced arthritis. MGP is bone-specific and involved in ossification, and the tissue in which it was predominantly identified in our sample material was subchondral bone. Other proteins identified in SF also originated from the articular tissues. Thrombospondin 1 (THBS1) was more abundant in cartilage, and the cartilage oligomeric matrix protein (COMP) and chondroadherin (CHAD) were more abundant in cartilage and subchondral bone. CHAD is involved in collagen organization and has previously been identified in the equine distal radius zone of Ranvier during normal chondrocyte differentiation. Based on results from in vitro studies, CHAD has been proposed to be involved in chronic inflammatory joint diseases in humans, but its role in equine arthritis and value as a specific biomarker will need further investigation.

Some proteins identified in the SF from joints with LPS-induced arthritis might originate from tissues outside the semiclosed joint environment. As examples, adiponectin D had a high abundance in adipose tissue, SERPINA7 displayed the highest abundance in the spleen, and the scavenger receptor cysteine rich family member with five domains (SSC5D) involved in the innate defense mechanisms was primarily identified in the intestine (jejunum, cecum, and colon). These proteins may accumulate in SF because of the inflammation-induced increases in the synovial membrane permeability. The concentrations of these proteins might also increase systemically upon release from the organs of origin and serve as systemic markers for joint inflammation.
Limitations of This Study

There are some limitations to our study. First, the study does not cover all very low abundance potentially tissue-specific proteins. This could have been achieved by the use of enrichment/depletion strategies, longer LC gradients, and/or by the use of fractionation but at the cost of more instrument time. Previous studies have shown that fractionation might benefit identification of low abundant proteins, but the number of identified peptide and protein groups was lower compared to the smaller nonfractionated libraries. Second, we observed many duplicate gene names. Although redundant sequences were deleted from the reference proteome before data analysis, many related, although not identical, sequences were identified and mapped to the same gene name (Supplementary File 5). These may reflect either different protein isoforms, potential point mutations, or lack of consensus about the sequence. The quality of the equine reference database is constantly improving and more proteins might become annotated and provide certainty about the protein sequences. Reanalysis of the data in some years might provide an even more extensive insight into the horse proteome and tissue distribution. The MS instrument selected for analysis also imposes a limitation. The hybrid quadrupole-orbitrap instrument Q Exactive HF-X used for analysis is less sensitive and has lower selectivity than the updated version, Orbitrap Exploris 480, and use of the latter might have increased the number of proteins identified. Employing a type of MS instrument that combines a linear ion trap with an orbitrap analyzer could also have affected both the number and type of proteins identified. The rapid advancements in MS technology keep improving the sensitivity and resolution of the instruments. At the time of sample analysis, the Q Exactive HF-X instrument used was state of the art and the instrument is still a valuable tool for high-throughput screening in proteomics. Another limitation of this study was the long storage time (~3 years) at -80  C for the SF samples from joints with LPS-induced experimental arthritis. This could have caused degradation of some proteins and potentially affected the results. However, optimal storage conditions (-80  C) and avoidance of repeated freeze-thaw cycles has been shown to preserve the proteins in bodily fluids intact for years. Due to the low number of individuals (n = 3), significance analyses were not performed. Yet, our results may still have biological relevance, and future studies may build on the proteomes identified and proteins highlighted as potential markers for disease. Lastly, we used a normalization method for global analysis that is known to reduce variation significantly. Data from many different tissues are very diverse in terms of protein numbers identified and abundance level, and VSN normalization is a statistical method aimed at making the sample variances nondependent from their mean intensities and bringing the samples onto a same scale, but with the consequence that log FCs are consistently underestimated. This means that the protein dynamics for global analysis might be compromised. On the other hand, use of nonimputed and median-normalized data as done in the other analyses included in this study might skew the protein abundance when comparing across different types of samples. To mitigate bias as much as possible, samples were prepared by the same person following the exact same protocol, and we trust that the findings highlighted are of biological relevance.
Conclusions

In conclusion, we present an extensive equine SL publicly available to enhance DIA-based data analysis in equine research. We demonstrated how the SL can advance our understanding of the tissue origin of proteins and how the different tissues influence the SF proteome in health and disease. The capability of the library to support the specific application for which the data set was intended and identification of potential biomarkers for tissue-specific diseases such as arthritis showcase the utility of the SL in equine research.

The MS data has been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE partner repository with the data set identifier PXD044741 and is publicly available.

passages.text: Association of plasma arachidonic acid levels with a bipolar disorder and the effects of a FADS gene variant

Recent genome-wide association studies (GWASs) have identified fatty acid desaturase (FADS) genes, which code key enzymes involved in polyunsaturated fatty acid (PUFA) desaturation as susceptibility genes for bipolar disorder (BD). Several quantitative changes in PUFAs suggest their involvement in BD pathogenesis. Therefore, this study aimed to clarify the relationship between BD and PUFAs by conducting lipidomics covariating with the FADS gene variant (rs174550), which is associated with PUFA levels and BD susceptibility. The concentrations of 23 fatty acids were measured using plasma samples from the BD group (n = 535) and the control group (n = 107). Differences in each PUFA concentration ratio were compared between the two groups. Also, differences in each PUFA concentration ratio were compared for each genotype in rs174550. Our results showed that the BD group had significantly lower concentrations of linoleic acid (LA) (beta = -0.36, p = 0.023) and arachidonic acid (AA) (beta = -0.18, p = 0.013) than the control group. Concerning the effect of FADS on the PUFA concentration ratio, carriers of C-allele at rs174550 had significantly decreased gamma-linolenic acid and AA concentration ratios. A previous GWAS reported that the presence of a C-allele at rs174550 increased the BD risk. This direction is consistent with the lipidomic results of the present study. In conclusion, both the FADS and BD were considered to regulate the AA concentration. Thus, as the FADS gene variant is crucial for conducting lipidomics of BD we believe that the allele frequency of FADS must be analyzed.
Introduction

Bipolar disorder (BD) is characterized by mood swings, with alternating mania and depression. Among mental disorders, the heritability of BD is approximately 70-80%, as high as that of schizophrenia. Mood stabilizers such as lithium salts and second-generation antipsychotics are used to treat BD; however, their pharmacological mechanism has not yet been elucidated. Moreover, the pathophysiology of BD is still unclear; thus, its elucidation is essential for the development of new treatments and prevention of BD.

Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs, n-3 PUFAs including alpha-linolenic acid [ALA], eicosapentaenoic acid [EPA], and docosahexaenoic acid [DHA] and n-6 PUFAs including linoleic acid [LA], gamma-linolenic acid [GLA], dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid [DGLA], and arachidonic acid [AA]) are possible novel treatment options. This speculation is based on several epidemiological, clinical, biomarker, and genomic evidence. For example, Noaghiul et al. reported a negative correlation between fish consumption and the lifetime prevalence of BD. In addition, clinical trials of PUFA supplementation in patients with BD have been conducted because n-3 PUFAs are safe and convenient to use. However, a clear conclusion has not been established. A recent meta-analysis showed that n-3 PUFA supplementation has beneficial effects on improving BD symptoms.

Lipidomics studies have reported that individuals with BD have a PUFA profile different from healthy controls although reports on the association between BD and changes in PUFA levels are not always consistent: Chiu et al. reported low plasma concentrations of AA and DHA in patients with BD, whereas Evans et al. revealed no significant difference in the plasma concentrations of AA, EPA, and DHA between the BD group and the control group. Koga et al. analyzed the largest sample size, reporting high plasma concentrations of n-6 PUFAs such as AA and low levels of n-3 PUFAs such as EPA and DHA in patients with BD. Such conflicting results are possibly caused by the small samples analyzed in each study, introducing inadequate statistical power.

Each of the n-3 and n-6 PUFA was biosynthesized by fatty acid desaturase (FADS1 and FADS2). ALA was metabolized to EPA and DHA by the FADS enzyme. Similarly, LA was metabolized to GLA, DGLA, and AA by the FADS enzyme (Supplementary Fig. 1). Recent genome-wide association studies (GWASs) have identified fatty acid desaturase (FADS1 and FADS2) genes, which encode enzymes involved in n-3 and n-6 lipid biosynthesis pathways, as susceptibility genes of BD (top single nucleotide polymorphism [SNP] rs28456). In addition, many studies of quantitative trait loci (QTL) have shown that FADS genes are associated with PUFA concentrations. In particular, Drajoo et al. reported that the concentrations of n-6 PUFAs (LA, GLA, DGLA, and AA) and n-3 PUFAs (ALA and EPA) were significantly related to FADS gene variants (i.e., LA rs174547, GLA rs174546, DGLA, rs174548, AA rs174577, ALA rs509360, and EPA rs174538). The effect size of variants on increasing or decreasing PUFA levels is modest compared with that of susceptibility for complex disorders, including BD. Interestingly, specific alleles that are associated with each PUFA levels are in tight linkage disequilibrium with BD susceptibility variants (i.e., the G allele of rs28456), indicating that low AA levels may be associated with susceptibility to BD.

Taken together, we speculate that the inconsistent results of lipidomics for BD may be induced by not considering the QTL effect of FADS gene variants. This study aimed to use lipidomics with a FADS gene-variant polymorphism as a covariate to examine the relationship between BD and PUFAs in the largest sample to date.
Methods
Subjects

The study recruited a total of 535 participants in the BD group and 107 in the control group from Fujita Health University and its affiliated hospitals. In the BD group, 179 of 535 individuals presented with type 1 BD (BD1), 313 with type 2 BD (BD2), and 43 with schizoaffective disorder (SA). In terms of clinical status, 117 individuals were in a depressive state, 28 in a manic state, and 390 were in remission. BD was diagnosed based on the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders 4th edition (DSM-IV) by at least two experienced psychiatrists using medical records and conducting unstructured interviews with the participants and their families. Individuals with known intellectual disabilities were excluded.

Written informed consent was obtained from all participants after they received a complete description of the study. This study was approved by the ethics committees of Fujita Health University and each participating hospital.
Fatty acid concentration measurement

Blood samples of the BD group were collected at the outpatient clinic, and plasma was extracted as soon as possible. In detail, vacuum tube blood collection was performed using Benoject II Vacuum Blood Collection Tubes VP-NA050K (containing EDTA-2Na), and 7 mL of blood was collected per tube. The blood samples were stored at 4  C. To measure fatty acid concentrations, samples were centrifuged at 1000 g for 10 min at 4  C to separate the plasma.

The separated plasma was stored at -80  C, and the following 23 types of saturated, monounsaturated, and polyunsaturated fatty acids were analyzed using a triple quadrupole gas chromatograph mass spectrometer GCMS-TQ8040 (SHIMADZU CORPORATION Kyoto, Japan): ALA, EPA, DHA, LA, GLA, DGLA, AA, lauric acid, myristic acid, myristoleic acid, pentadecanoic acid, palmitic acid, palmitoleic acid, margaric acid, heptadecanoic acid, stearic acid, oleic acid, nonadecanic acid, arachidic acid, eicosenoic acid, eicosadienoic acid, behenic acid, and lignoceric acid.

passages.text: To consider changes in the concentration of all fatty acids that fluctuate with diet and match the outcome of the previously reported QTL analysis, the fatty acid concentration ratio (each fatty acid concentration/total fatty acid concentration) was calculated from the measured fatty acid concentration. In this study, the n-3 and n-6 PUFAs (ALA, EPA, DHA, LA, GLA, DGLA, and AA) were measured and used as primary outcomes in the analysis. Further, other fatty acids were measured to calculate the concentration ratios.
Genotyping

Typing was performed using Illumina HumanOmniExpressExome 1.2 chip for 520 subjects of the BD group and 72 subjects of the controls group. In addition, 15 subjects of the BD group and 35 subjects of the control group were further genotyped for rs174550 (FADS gene) using the TaqMan probe method. rs174550 was selected because rs174550 and top SNPs of a previous report are in nearly absolute linkage disequilibrium (i.e., LA rs174547, R2 = 0.999; GLA rs174546, R2 = 0.999; DGLA rs174548, R2 = 1.0; AA rs174577, R2 = 0.9372; ALA rs509360, R2 = 0.9785; EPA rs174538, R2 = 1.0).
Statistical analysis

First, a simple linear regression analysis was conducted using the diagnosis (BD group/control group) and rs174550 as independent variables. Next, multiple linear regression analysis was performed to compare the difference in PUFAs between the BD group and the control group. This analysis is the main analysis of this study. The ratio of each fatty acid (concentration of each PUFA/total fatty acid concentration) was used as the dependent variable. The independent variables included diagnosis (BD group /control group: primary outcome), sex, BMI, age, postprandial time (minutes), 4  C storage time (minutes), hemolysis (yes/no), chyle (yes/no), dyslipidemia (yes/no), diabetes (yes/no), hypertension (yes/no), and rs174550 (CC/CT/TT). The level of significance was set at p < 0.05. The significance level for rs174550 was set at the level for the genome-wide significance (p < 5.0 x 10-8) because previous studies referenced while selecting rs174550 were genome-wide association analyses; thus, we matched that level accordingly. Linear regression analyses were performed using R version 3.6.3.

Table 1 shows participants' backgrounds. Significant differences between the BD group and control group were observed in, age, postprandial time, BMI, sex, and dyslipidemia status, all of which were covariates in the main analysis. Supplementary Table 1 shows the fatty acid concentration ratios and concentrations analyzed. Supplementary Table 2 depicts the results of the simple linear regression analysis of PUFA concentration ratio and diagnosis, PUFA concentration ratio, and rs174550. Table 2 shows the results of the diagnosis (BD group/control group):the primary outcome in this study:and of rs174550 (CC/CT/TT) in the multiple linear regression analysis. Supplementary Table 3 shows all multiple linear regression analysis results.

The diagnostic status was significantly associated with the concentration ratios of LA (beta = -0.36, p = 0.023) and AA (beta = -0.18, p = 0.013) in multiple linear regression analysis. These results indicated that the BD group had significantly lower LA and AA concentration ratios. For other PUFAs, no association was found between BD diagnosis and concentration ratios.

The QTL SNP (rs174550), which was reported in previous studies, was significantly associated with the concentration ratios of GLA (beta = -0.079, p < 2.0 x 10-16) and AA (beta = -0. 36, p < 2.0 x 10-16). These mean that patients with the C-allele in rs174550, which was a risk allele of BD, had significantly lower concentration ratios of GLA and AA than those with the T-allele. However, compared with the findings of previous studies, other PUFAs were not associated with the genotypes in rs174550.
Discussion

In this study, the BD group had significantly lower concentration ratios of LA and AA based on the analysis that took into account the QTL effect of SNP. This indicates the independent diagnostic effect of specific PUFAs on BD susceptibility. Furthermore, we conducted an ad hoc analysis to determine if the associations between PUFA and diagnosis differed depending on the BD subtype (BD1/BD2/SA) or status (depressive/manic/remission). Supplementary method 1 presents the detailed analysis methods. These results are shown in Supplementary Tables 4 and 5. Regarding the association between subtypes and LA, significant associations were found for BD1 and SA, with the same effect direction as observed in the overall BD group. Although BD2 was not significant, it showed the same effect direction. For AA, all subtypes showed significant associations with the same effect direction as observed in the overall BD group. Regarding the association between statuses and LA, significant associations were observed for all statuses, with the same effect direction as observed in the overall BD group. Regarding AA, significant associations were found in remission and manic statuses, with the same effect direction as observed in the overall BD group. Although the association with depressive status was not significant, it showed the same effect direction. Considerably, the effects of LA and AA observed in the overall BD group analysis are probably common across all BD subtypes or statuses.

This figure shows that both the QTL effect of SNP (reduction in AA by genotype) and the diagnostic effect are independently involved in the BD risk by low AA concentration.

In the previous GWAS targeting BD, the C-allele of rs174550 was the risk allele for BD (OR = 1.17, p = 1.2 x 10-8). This finding supported the result that low GLA and AA concentrations in individuals harboring the C-allele were associated with BD, although other PUFAs, such as DHA and EPA, were not risk factors for BD. This also clarified the finding that BD risk by low AA concentration was explained both by the QTL effect of the SNP (decreased AA by genotype) and the diagnostic effect, which were independent of each other (AA, beta = 0.070, p = 0.45; Fig. 1). By contrast, the low LA concentration was not influenced by the QTL effect but is mainly explained by the diagnostic effect. Such "non-significant" QTL effect is reasonable because LA concentration is mainly determined by diet (i.e., LA cannot be synthesized in the body), is in the upstream of the n-6 pathway, and is metabolized into GLA (significant QTL effect), DGLA, and AA (significant QTL effect) by FADS.

Compared with previous lipidomics studies of BD (Table 4), the sample size in the present study is one of the largest and thus provided the most powerful results. However, we could not obtain concordant and conclusive results similar to other studies because the sample size was not large enough to deny type I and II errors. In addition, previous studies did not consider the QTL effect of the FADS SNP, which is also a susceptible SNP to BD. Such a small sample size induces variable allele frequencies either in cases or controls, which may influence the QTL effect on PUFAs. Therefore, the QTL effect is one of the most important confounding factors when interpreting the lipidomics for BD.

passages.text: The strength of this study is attributed to the largest sample size, and the "abnormality" of AA concentration is a good reason to explore the causal effect on BD susceptibility because the QTL effect was concordant with those in other QTL studies. Because QTLs in other PUFAs, except GLA and AA, were not replicated in this study, we speculated the following reasons: (1) the sample size was small to detect the QTL effect and (2) previous QTL results showed that the direction of the effect on DGLA in rs174550 was contrasting between Caucasians and Han Chinese, which suggest population difference in the effect of rs174550 on DGLA. However, as mentioned above, we replicated the QTL effect of the SNP on AA and GLA, concordant with other large QTL analyses, and thus concluded concrete results at least for AA.

We believe that AA is important in elucidating the pathogenesis of BD because several associations between AA metabolism and BD were reported so far. According to reports, antipsychotics, and mood stabilizers such as lithium salts, valproate, carbamazepine, and lamotrigine affected AA metabolism in the brain via N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors and D2 receptors, which the authors called the "arachidonic cascade hypothesis." In this hypothesis, plasma AA is consumed in BD because of increased AA metabolism in the brain, and mood stabilizers decrease the turnover of AA in several brain phospholipids. Even in accordance with this hypothesis, as our study revealed compatible results that the plasma AA concentrations decreased, it supported the finding that impaired AA metabolism affects the pathogenesis of BD. Therefore, further studies investigating AA metabolism in the brain are essential and may elucidate the pathogenesis of BD.

To interpret this result, we stress important limitations. We could not control the effect of diet. Although we included the time from the last diet as a covariate in the model and applied the ratio (e.g., AA/all PUFAs) to control the diet, we could not follow the contents of the diet, and such is associated with PUFAs located in the upstream of this pathway (such as LA). Further studies should be performed to examine dietary intake and items that can be included in multiple linear regression analyses. Moreover, the effects of dyslipidemia and diabetes medications on PUFA concentrations have not been elucidated. However, these medications are important for the evaluation of PUFA levels. This is because dyslipidemia medications can affect cholesterol and triglyceride levels, and some diabetes treatments can affect lipid levels. Supplementary Tables 6 and 7 present the breakdown of dyslipidemia and diabetes medications. We included information on dyslipidemia and diabetes in our analysis as they may influence blood lipid levels. However, treatment medications were not included in the analysis. This is because most patients with dyslipidemia were taking treatment medications. Similarly, most patients with diabetes were also on their medication. Treatment medication information was excluded from the analysis due to the strong correlation between dyslipidemia and its treatment medication (r = 0.97), as well as diabetes and its treatment medication (r = 0.95). To examine the impact of dyslipidemia and diabetes medications on PUFA concentrations, further research specifically targeting these medications must be performed. In addition, several participants in the BD group were taking mood stabilizers, antipsychotics, or both in this study. Therefore, the effects of these medications on PUFA were examined in this study. Supplementary Table 8 shows the types of mood stabilizers and antipsychotics used. To examine the effects of these medications on PUFA, a multiple linear regression analysis was conducted using groups taking antipsychotics (AP), lithium salts (Li), and anticonvulsants (AC) and a group not taking any of these medications. Supplementary method 2 and Supplementary Table 9 present the detailed analysis methods and results. The group not taking any of these medications was considered the reference group (no-medication group). The beta (beta) coefficients of the concentration ratio of PUFA in groups taking AP (AP group), Li (Li group), AC (AC group), both AP and Li (AP + Li group), AP and AC (AP + AC group), Li and AC (Li + AC group) and AP, Li, and AC (AP + Li + AC group) were calculated. In particular, we focused on LA and AA, where significant associations were observed in the main analysis under the diagnostic categories of the independent variables. For LA, the AP and Li groups had positive beta coefficients. The AC group and the two or more medications group had negative beta coefficients, with a relatively large beta coefficient and significant association observed particularly in the AP + Li + AC group. This finding indicates that the concomitant use of AP, Li, and AC decreased the LA concentration ratios. The effect of the diagnosis in reducing the LA concentration ratios observed in the main analysis may have been enhanced by the effect of reducing the LA concentration ratios present in the two or more medications group. However, understanding why a negative beta coefficient was observed in the AP + Li group despite the positive beta coefficients in the AP and Li groups, as well as why this trend is most pronounced in the AP + Li + AC group, is difficult. Furthermore, no studies have reported a relationship between these medications and LA so far. The effects of medications used in BD on LA should be clarified in future research with larger sample sizes. Regarding AA, there were no notably large beta coefficients among the groups, nor were there any significant associations with AA. Therefore, the relationship between medications and AA was not clarified.

In conclusion, the BD group has significantly lower AA and LA concentration ratios than the control group. In addition, a strong QTL effect of the FADS SNP was found on AA and GLA; however, such an effect was independent of BD susceptibility. Therefore, AA and LA are good candidates for susceptibility to BD, and such QTL effect of the SNP should be included as a covariate to interpret the lipidomics for BD.
