In the subgroup analysis evaluating the impact of type of surgery on patient outcome, 19,885 participants were included (Supplementary Appendix, Table S2). Females with prior knee joint replacement surgery or knee joint arthroscopy in the index knee had a statistically significant smaller pain reduction compared to those without prior knee surgery, but according to the responder analysis, the between-group differences were not considered clinically relevant (Table 3). The results from the sensitivity analysis (n, 18,019) evaluating the impact of prior surgery in any of the four joints on outcome measures were similar to the results from the main analysis (Supplementary Appendix, Table S3). Also, restricting the analysis to patients enrolled during the last 5 years showed similar results (not shown).
Discussion

We found that about one in four patients with knee OA enrolled in a supervised patient education and exercise therapy program (GLA:D ) had previous surgery in the most affected knee joint. Patients with prior knee surgery did not experience clinically relevant inferior change in knee pain, joint related quality of life, and walking speed after participation in the intervention, compared to those without previous knee surgery.

One in four patients who was enrolled in the patient education and exercise therapy program previously had knee surgery, which is in line with results among patients participating in the Swedish "Better management of patients with OsteoArthritis" (BOA) program. Also, we found that those with prior knee surgery were more likely to be male, have a history of previous knee injury, experience longer duration of joint symptoms, and were more likely to have a high physical activity level. These findings correspond to the elevated risk of knee OA in people with prior knee injury, as a knee injury is a typical reason for knee surgery, and that incidence of knee injuries is higher among males, particularly due to their greater involvement in sports activities. Paradoxically, knee OA patients with prior knee injury tend to have more pronounced OA symptoms, longer symptom duration, and general better health status, and in the current study, we confirmed that this also applies to those with prior knee surgery. Nevertheless, we found that those with prior knee surgery did not differ from those without prior surgery in terms of treatment outcomes from the GLA:D  program.

Although we did observe a statistically significant between-group difference in change in knee pain in females in favor of the no surgery group, it was only small and not supported by evaluations of the other outcomes or in males, nor considered clinically relevant. As such, previous knee surgery did not influence patient outcomes, which is consistent with the results from a study evaluating factors associated with the outcome in a similar intervention delivered in the BOA program in Sweden, where they found a statistically significant but small association between previous surgery and pain reduction at 3 months in favor of those without previous surgery. Notably, the association was stronger when evaluating the pain reduction 12 months after baseline, which was not evaluated in the current study. Extending previous research, our study evaluated the influence of type of surgery as well as the impact of a surgery in any knee/hip joint stratified by sex but did not observe any clinically important between-group differences. Previously, a range of different factors has been studied as potential moderators of the effect of exercise therapy targeting people with knee OA, but in general, there is a lack of ability to identify factors that significantly modify the effect which was also the case for prior surgery in the current study.

The target group for the GLA:D  program is people with knee or hip osteoarthritis, thus typically not patients with previous joint replacement surgery in the joint for which they seek care. However, joint replacement surgery is not an explicit exclusion criterion for enrollment, and therefore, a small proportion of GLA:D  participants (0.5%) have had a previous joint replacement surgery in the most affected joint. Around 15 to 20% develop chronic pain after a joint replacement surgery which might explain their participation in the GLA:D  program. In the current study, those with a previous knee joint replacement surgery in the most affected joint experience a lower degree of pain relief, compared to those without previous surgery even though the confidence intervals are wide and the magnitude of the between-group difference in patients reaching the MIC did not exceed the a priori defined threshold for clinical relevance. People with chronic pain after prior joint replacement surgery might have an inferior pain relief compared to those without previous surgery, which may be due to that exercise therapy does not seem to have an additional effect on chronic pain in addition to patient education in this population.

We showed that a large part of the population engaging in a patient education and exercise therapy program targeting knee OA symptoms had a previous knee surgery. Thus, the results from our study are valuable for future healthcare planning as it suggest that the change in knee pain, joint related quality of life, and walking speed in patients with knee OA after guideline-recommended treatments is not moderated by previous surgery status. This knowledge can be valuable for both patients and clinicians when discussing and managing treatment expectations as people with knee osteoarthritis and prior knee surgery can be informed to expect an average outcome from a supervised patient education and exercise therapy program.

The strengths of this study are the large sample size and that we included patients with knee OA from a large clinical cohort, likely with good generalizability to a primary care clinical setting. The information on previous surgery was self-reported and might be prone to recall error and thereby the risk of misclassification; however, the self-reported information on prior surgery has previously been shown to have a moderate agreement with registry-based data, i.e., a perfect agreement between self-report and registry-based data for joint replacement surgery and lower agreement with less invasive knee surgeries. Nevertheless, a risk of misclassification in the current study still exists, potentially underestimating the between-group differences. We were only able to classify patients into few categories according to types of surgeries, which prevented us from analyzing if the results differ according to more detailed information on types of surgeries. Finally, information about time between surgery and enrollment in GLA:D  was not available; thus, we were unable to take this into account in the analyses and interpretation of data. An absolute difference of 20% was a priory defined as between-group differences to be considered clinically relevant. In lack of consensus-based thresholds, this was an arbitrary level that was found to be reasonable; thus, it can be questioned whether an alternative threshold would have been more appropriate. Given the observational nature of the study, it is not possible to ascertain how large a part of the observed changes that are due to the GLA:D  intervention, regression-to-the-mean, or contextual factors. Also due to the temporality of the data collection, we were only able to take sex into account in the analyses, thus residual confounding may occur.

In conclusion, we observed no clinically relevant differences in treatment outcomes in pain, joint related quality of life, and walking speed following a supervised patient education and exercise therapy program regardless of previous knee surgery status. These results suggest that previous knee surgery does not impact the potential benefit of exercise therapy and patient education as effective strategies for managing symptoms and enhancing function in patients with knee OA.

passages.text: Medical image segmentation with UNet-based multi-scale context fusion

Histopathological examination holds a crucial role in cancer grading and serves as a significant reference for devising individualized patient treatment plans in clinical practice. Nevertheless, the distinctive features of numerous histopathological image targets frequently contribute to suboptimal segmentation performance. In this paper, we propose a UNet-based multi-scale context fusion algorithm for medical image segmentation, which extracts rich contextual information by extracting semantic information at different encoding stages and assigns different weights to the semantic information at different scales through TBSFF module to improve the learning ability of the network for features. Through multi-scale context fusion and feature selection networks, richer semantic features and detailed information are extracted. The target can be more accurately segmented without significantly increasing the extra overhead. The results demonstrate that our algorithm achieves superior Dice and IoU scores with a relatively small parameter count. Specifically, on the GlaS dataset, the Dice score is 90.56, and IoU is 83.47. For the MoNuSeg dataset, the Dice score is 79.07, and IoU is 65.98.
Introduction

Pathological examinations are typically conducted by pathologists who scrutinize stained specimens through a microscope, a process demanding extensive medical expertise and professional training. Throughout this examination, pathologists must concentrate on pivotal areas of significance within tissue samples, alongside randomly selected sub-areas. Subsequently, they render judgments to ascertain whether the sample is normal or pathological. However, histopathological images frequently encompass a multitude of targets, presenting a challenge for traditional image segmentation algorithms that tend to exhibit subpar performance in handling such images. With the revival and prosperity of deep learning technology in the field of computer vision, the application of methods such as image classification, image segmentation, image positioning and application based on deep learning in natural scenes and medical imaging has also increased dramatically. The widespread adoption of deep learning in medical imaging owes to its proficiency in image interpretation and classification, offering innovative approaches to medical image segmentation. Medical image segmentation stands as a pivotal technology for the analysis and comprehension of medical images, delivering crucial auxiliary information for clinicians in diagnosis, treatment, and contributing significantly to disease monitoring and predicting treatment outcomes. In tandem with the rapid advancements in medical imaging technology, histopathology has experienced substantial progress, marked by the increasing prevalence of deep learning applications in medical image segmentation. This trend provides a promising solution for the intricate task of segmenting numerous targets in histopathology.

Among various network models, UNet stands out as the most widely used encoder-decoder model for medical image segmentation. The encoder captures low and high semantic features, while the decoder reconstructs the final result by leveraging these captured features. To recover spatial information lost during pooling, skip connections are employed. However, current state-of-the-art semantic segmentation methods often rely on simple merging of low-semantic features from different levels, lacking effective extraction of the most informative parts from various semantic levels.

UNet++, a well-known variant of the UNet network, addresses this limitation by narrowing the semantic gap between the encoder and decoder. It achieves this by introducing dense skip connections that incorporate more low-semantic features from the encoder into the decoder, leading to improved segmentation performance. This method increases the number of skip connections and maximizes the fusion of low-semantic features with other semantic features of the same size.

An alternative approach involves the use of Transformer-based methods, with UCTransNet being a notable representative. Instead of simply merging low-semantic information from the encoder with high-semantic information from the decoder via skip connections, this approach first passes the low-semantic information through two Transformer-based modules, CCT (Channel Cross fusion with Transformer) and CCA (Channel-wise Cross-Attention). These modules perform fusion of different levels of semantic information concurrently and exhibit similarities to channel attention mechanisms.

The skip connections in the network are redesigned to achieve efficient use of features, thereby ensuring that the features of the input image can be effectively transferred to the decoder module for further processing and analysis.

TBSFF (three-branch feature fusion network): The TBSFF module serves as a dynamic selection mechanism, enhancing segmentation effectiveness by extracting pertinent information from the three input branches with varying degrees of attention. This proposed TBSFF module facilitates the fusion of multi-scale features, which are subsequently transmitted to the encoder module. Such an approach significantly augments the model's capability to capture information across various scales.

Performance evaluation: Through experiments conducted on the MoNuSeg and GlaS public medical datasets, we assess the performance of TBSFF-UNet. Particularly, we select a subset of challenging images and observe that TBSFF-UNet exhibits a significant improvement over UNet when applied to these specific cases.

While previous methods have demonstrated notable improvements in image segmentation performance, they often come with a substantial increase in model parameters and struggle to effectively extract crucial information from low semantic features. We contend that the UNet encoder alone is adept at feature extraction. However, the primary limitation of UNet lies in its skip connections. Thus, we propose the TBSFF-UNet (Three-Branch Feature Fusion UNet) model, which introduces novel skip connections to integrate diverse semantic levels. This facilitates the aggregation of information, enabling the capture of richer semantic details even at lower feature layers, subsequently forwarded to the decoder module for deeper analysis and processing. Additionally, we introduce a three-branch feature fusion module (TBSFF) for selecting semantic information from different levels. Employing a dynamic selection mechanism, the TBSFF module enhances segmentation performance by extracting pertinent information from the three input branches with varying degrees of attention. Our contributions can be summarized as follows:
Related works

Long et al. were the pioneers in introducing a fully convolutional network. This groundbreaking approach replaced the fully connected layer of traditional convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with deconvolution operations, enabling pixel-level predictions for images. The advent of fully convolutional networks in the realm of image semantic segmentation has played a pivotal role in advancing the field of image segmentation and has yielded remarkable outcomes, particularly in the domain of medical image segmentation.

Ronnebergerder et al. proposed the widely recognized UNet architecture, which remains a cornerstone in the field of medical image segmentation. The UNet model comprises two key components: an encoder and a decoder. The encoder consists of five stages, where basic convolution operations are applied, followed by ReLU activation function. Subsequently, a 2  2 pooling operation is employed to downsample the image for the first four stages. In the decoder, the encoded features are utilized, and an upsampling operation is performed to gradually recover the spatial and detailed information of the image. By extending the fully convolutional network, the UNet model enhances the network depth, progressively reduces the size of the feature map through additional convolutional layers, and effectively integrates contextual information using skip connections. This novel network structure has garnered significant attention, leading to the proposal of various modified architectures based on UNet.

Drawing inspiration from the UNet network, Zhou et al. introduced the UNet++ structure, which represents a more potent architecture for medical image segmentation. The fundamental essence of this architecture remains the classic encoder-decoder network. However, unlike the original UNet, the UNet++ network incorporates a series of nested dense skip connections. These redesigned skip connections exploit feature maps from the encoder more effectively, thereby reducing the semantic gap between the encoder and decoder. Consequently, the model captures fine-grained image details, leading to improved segmentation outcomes. Building upon the UNet++ architecture, Zhou et al. further enhanced the skip connections to aggregate features of different semantic scales within the decoder sub-network, resulting in a highly flexible feature fusion scheme.

In addition to UNet and UNet++, other innovative architectures have been proposed in the field of medical image segmentation. For instance, Alom et al. introduced the R2U-Net network, which combines the advantages of U-Net, residual networks, and recurrent CNNs. This architecture leverages residual connections to increase network depth and recurrent CNNs to extract feature information more effectively from images. The R2U-Net demonstrates superior performance over UNet in various tasks such as blood vessel segmentation, skin cancer segmentation, and lung lesion segmentation in retinal images. Similarly, Oktay et al. presented an attention-based model named attention U-Net for medical image segmentation. This model automatically learns to prioritize objects of different shapes and sizes, assigning different weights to relevant and irrelevant regions. By highlighting the useful features of relevant regions and suppressing the invalid features of unrelated regions, the attention U-Net improves model accuracy without significantly increasing computational costs.

Although these architectures exhibit certain differences, they collectively demonstrate the value of reducing the semantic discrepancy between the encoder and decoder through skip connections, leading to improved performance of the UNet model. However, it is important to note that introducing excessive skip connections may result in increased network complexity and a larger model size. With the integration of Transformer architecture into computer vision, the introduction of Vision Transformer (ViT) has yielded remarkable results on various image recognition benchmarks, such as ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and VTAB. By applying the Transformer's self-attention mechanism to image classification, ViT has achieved superior performance. Inspired by ViT's success in computer vision, several Transformer-based models for image segmentation have emerged. TransUNet was the first Transformer-based medical image segmentation model, combining the strengths of Transformer and UNet. The model utilizes Transformer to encode tokenized image patches from CNN feature maps, extracting global contextual information. Additionally, the encoder performs an upsampling operation on the feature map after the Transformer, which is then combined with the CNN-encoded feature map to gradually restore the spatial and detailed information of the image. Valanarasu et al. introduced Med Transformer, a Transformer-based model that incorporates a gated axial-attention mechanism in the self-attention module. The architecture includes an additional control mechanism, facilitating efficient computation of context information and enabling long-range interactions in feature map encoding. The authors also proposed a local-global training strategy, employing two branches: a local branch for detailed information at the original image resolution and a global branch for high-level information. This approach achieves promising results across three different datasets.

Cao et al. presented Swin-Unet, a pure Transformer-based model similar to UNet. Swin-Unet utilizes a hierarchical Transformer with a shifted window as a decoder to extract contextual features, replacing the convolutional layers in the UNet network. The model also incorporates a Transformer-based decoder to perform the deconvolution operation and recover spatial information in the feature map. By designing skip connections, the model achieves effective contextual information interaction, demonstrating favorable results on multi-organ and cardiac segmentation datasets. Wang et al. proposed the UCTransNet model, comprising a multi-scale cross-channel fusion (CCT) and an effectively connected cross-channel attention interaction sub-module (CCA) for guiding fusion. The model incorporates attention mechanisms and leverages the CCT and CCA modules as replacements for the skip connections in the UNet network. UCTransNet has achieved promising results on the GlaS, MoNuSeg, and Synapse datasets. Wang et al. introduced the Swin Deformable Attention Hybrid UNet (SDAH-UNet) model, incorporating the Swin Deformable model. This model not only enhances segmentation performance but also offers a more direct interpretation for convolutional and multi-head self-attention mechanisms. Liao et al. proposed the Transformer-based Annotation-Bias-Aware (TAB) model, which addresses annotation bias by considering bias in the labeling process. The model models the relationship between annotators' preferences and random errors to mitigate annotator-related biases. To overcome the "token-flatten" challenge associated with the direct utilization of the Transformer, He et al. introduced U-Nermer. This method involves segmenting the input image into local patches, with the global contextual information among these patches being learned through the self-attention mechanism employed by Transformer and UNet.

The proposal of these networks has extensively promoted the development of medical image segmentation technology. Unfortunately, these networks generally have the problems of large models, large model parameters, and large FlOPs, and it is difficult to achieve a good relationship between the effect and the model complexity balance.
Proposed network architecture: TBSFF-UNet
Overall architecture

U-Net stands as a cornerstone in medical image segmentation, garnering significant attention from researchers. In the realm of histological image segmentation, numerous scholars have endeavored to enhance U-Net at various levels. Yet, to our knowledge, existing improvements to U-Net predominantly concentrate on bolstering its encoder. For instance, TransUNet adopts a simplistic approach by integrating Transformer into U-Net's encoder module, while Swin-UNet pioneers the introduction of Swin Transformer to replace the convolution block in U-Net, forming the first U-shaped architecture purely based on Transformer. However, we maintain that merely integrating Transformer into U-Net to enhance the encoder's information extraction capability may not yield optimal network performance. Instead, it tends to exacerbate model complexity, taxing computational resources and impeding network training. We posit that U-Net's encoder suffices for feature extraction. The principal bottleneck in U-Net's efficacy lies in its skip connections. Therefore, our proposed TBSFF-UNet model seeks to ameliorate network performance by refining skip connections without substantially augmenting model complexity.

In this work, we propose a novel network architecture, termed TBSFF-UNet, illustrated in Fig. 1. The network comprises an encoder, decoder, and feature fusion module. The encoder learns from input images, extracts features through encoding at different stages, and transmits them to both the decoder module and the TBSFF module through skip connections. TBSFF-UNet redefines skip connections in the network to efficiently utilize features.
Illustration of the proposed TBSFF-UNet.

By designing a new network structure, TBSFF-UNet optimizes the feature transfer between the encoder and decoder. The TBSFF-UNet module then performs multi-branch feature fusion on different features, extracting more critical features. During this process, TBSFF employs a kernel selection mechanism to model features from different levels passed between the encoder and decoder. It generates different weights to adjust and fuse features from different levels, producing new and more effective features for improved segmentation results. Importantly, TBSFF-UNet achieves enhanced segmentation performance without significantly increasing model parameters and computational complexity, thereby ensuring model efficiency alongside improved segmentation outcomes.
Redesigned skip connection path

In the U-Net architecture, the encoder's features are passed to the decoder through skip connections, effectively reducing the semantic gap between the encoder and decoder. In U-Net++, the encoder's feature maps undergo dense convolutional blocks, and a substantial number of skip connections are employed to transmit high-resolution features from the encoder to the decoder, enhancing the proximity of semantic features between the encoder and decoder. However, this approach significantly increases the model's complexity. In the context of histological image segmentation tasks, we observed that more skip connections do not necessarily lead to better results; instead, it is crucial to design appropriate skip connections.

In this work, we present the TBSFF-UNet network, a modification of the U-Net architecture that redefines skip connections, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Compared to U-Net++, TBSFF-UNet reduces the number of skip connections considerably. It achieves this by transmitting the feature maps from both the encoder and the partially decoded feature maps from the decoder to the TBSFF module. This process aids in extracting effective features, thereby enhancing segmentation precision. Figure 1 also demonstrates that TBSFF-UNet's skip connections, in comparison to U-Net++, only introduce a limited number of additional connections.

Furthermore, the skip connections designed in this study not only transmit features from the corresponding decoder stages in the encoder to the decoder but also convey features from the previous and subsequent encoder stages to the TBSFF module. This approach enables the transfer of more low-level, high-resolution features to TBSFF, helping alleviate spatial information loss caused by the encoding stage.
Redesigned selective kernel networks
Illustration of the proposed TBSFF.

The TBSFF-UNet model proposed in this paper does not simply concatenate the features passed through skip connections from the encoder and the features from the decoder. Instead, it employs a selectively designed three-branch fusion module for merging the input three feature maps, known as TBSFF, as depicted in Fig. 2. This module represents a dynamic selection mechanism where attention to different branches varies. The selective convolution is achieved through the Fuse and Select operations, implementing a mechanism for dynamic feature fusion.

Experiments
Datasets

We assess the performance of our proposed model using the gland segmentation benchmark datasets: GlaS and MoNuSeg. The GlaS dataset comprises 165 images from T3 and T4 stages of 16 H &E stained tissue sections of colorectal adenocarcinoma. It consists of the Training Part, Test Part A, and Test Part B. For this study, 85 images from the training part are utilized for training, while 80 images from test parts A and B are employed for testing. The MoNuSeg dataset comprises 44 images, with 30 designated for training and 14 for testing. These images capture a variety of nuclear appearances from different patients, disease states, and organs, and the dataset includes over 21,000 meticulously annotated nuclear boundaries.
Implementation details

The network model was implemented using PyTorch, with hardware consisting of dual Intel Xeon E5-2678 v3 @ 2.50GHz CPUs, 32 GB of RAM, and a single Nvidia RTX 3080 GPU card with 10GB of VRAM. For the Glas and MoNuSeg datasets, the batch size was set to 4, the number of epochs was set to 2000, and early stopping was configured after 200 epochs. The input resolution was set to 224  224, patch size was set to 16, and the Adam optimizer was used with a learning rate of 0.001. Binary cross-entropy and dice loss functions were employed as the training loss functions. To ensure experiment reproducibility, CUDA and Python seeds were set. The evaluation during the experiment used the dice coefficient and Intersection over Union (IOU) as performance metrics. To eliminate the randomness of a single experiment, a fivefold cross-validation was conducted, and the results were averaged, along with calculating the standard deviation.

Discussion

Medical image segmentation plays a vital role in the field of digital pathology. This paper proposes a contextual information fusion-based TBSFF-UNet network to provide a stable and reliable medical image segmentation method. It is validated on the GlaS and MoNuSeg benchmark datasets, and achieves a 90.56 dice coefficient and 83.47IoU on the dataset and 79.07dice and 65.98IoU on the MoNuSeg dataset. The network designed in this paper successfully extracts more effective information from the feature map by the encoder and narrows the semantic gap of contextual information. The advantages of the proposed model are demonstrated through rich experiments and in-depth analysis.

However, the model in this paper still has some shortcomings. For example, when the samples are seriously unbalanced, the algorithm's performance is general. In the future, we will solve this problem by integrating Transformer and GAN networks into the network.

passages.text: Fabry Disease in a Female: A Unique Case Highlighting the Variability in Clinical Presentation

Fabry disease is a rare X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by mutations in the GLA gene, leading to deficient activity of the enzyme alpha-galactosidase A. This enzyme deficiency results in the accumulation of globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) in various tissues, causing multi-systemic manifestations. This case report presents a rare instance of Fabry disease in a 32-year-old female patient, highlighting the unique clinical presentation with multisystem involvement. Fabry disease is an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder that primarily affects males, while females are often considered asymptomatic carriers. Heterozygous females can exhibit a broad spectrum of clinical manifestations, varying from a complete absence of symptoms to the full expression of the disease. The patient presented with a complex array of symptoms, including progressive dyspnea, fever, headache, lower limb pain, and periorbital edema, accompanied by a history of hypertension and chronic kidney disease (CKD). Laboratory investigations revealed severe anemia, elevated renal function parameters, and significant proteinuria. A renal biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of Fabry disease, based on the characteristic histopathological findings of widespread glomerular and segmental tuft sclerosis, as well as podocyte enlargement with fine vacuolization. The patient was managed with a combination of sequential hemodialysis and diuretic therapy. This case is a rare and unique example of Fabry disease in a female patient, with symptoms affecting multiple organ systems, including the renal, cardiovascular, and neurological systems. It underscores the importance of maintaining a high index of suspicion for Fabry disease, even in female patients, and the need for a comprehensive diagnostic approach to ensure timely diagnosis and appropriate management. Early recognition of this rare condition in females is crucial for the implementation of targeted therapies, such as enzyme replacement therapy and oral chaperone therapy, to prevent the progression of multi-organ damage.
Introduction

Fabry disease, an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder, arises from a deficiency or absence of alpha-galactosidase A (alpha-GAL A) activity. This enzymatic dysfunction is attributed to genetic mutations in the GLA (galactosidase alpha) gene, located at Xq21.3-q22, resulting in the lysosomal accumulation of glycosphingolipids, predominantly cerebroside trihexoside. Consequently, affected individuals exhibit a significantly elevated risk of developing ischaemic stroke, small-fiber peripheral neuropathy, cardiac dysfunction, and chronic kidney disease (CKD). The estimated prevalence of Fabry disease is approximately one in 40,000 individuals. However, newborn screening suggests a higher incidence of 1:3, 100 to 1:1500 male births. The disease affects all ethnic groups, with males more severely affected than females.

Historically, females were considered to be asymptomatic carriers of defective GLA genes who were not vulnerable to the symptoms and vital organ abnormalities. However, recent research has revealed that heterozygous females can exhibit a broad spectrum of clinical presentations, ranging from the complete absence of symptoms to a full manifestation of the classic disease. This variability in disease expression may be attributed, at least partially, to skewed X-chromosome inactivation. This process could lead to a higher proportion of cells expressing the disease-causing mutation in affected organs, resulting in more severe clinical outcomes. Hypertension is frequently observed in Fabry disease patients, primarily due to progressive renal impairment. Both diagnosis and management of Fabry disease present considerable challenges as the disease presents with a broad spectrum of clinical manifestations, ranging from early-onset, severe forms to later-onset variants primarily affecting the heart and kidneys. Early diagnosis and enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) or chaperone therapy are crucial in mitigating organ damage and improving long-term outcomes. However, when organ-specific symptoms are evaluated in isolation, the underlying systemic etiology may be overlooked.

We present a rare case of Fabry disease in a female patient, exemplifying the intricate interplay between molecular pathology and multisystem clinical manifestations. The resultant deficiency or dysfunction of alpha-galactosidase A in this patient leads to the progressive accumulation of globotriaosylceramide within lysosomes, primarily affecting the vascular endothelium, kidneys, myocardium, and nervous system.
Case presentation

A 32-year-old female with a known history of hypertension and CKD presented to the emergency department with a complex array of symptoms. The patient's chief complaints included progressive dyspnea over a 10-day period, low-grade to moderate fever (100 F to 102 F) for four days, and a three-month history of headache, lower limb pain, and periorbital edema. Her past medical history was significant for oliguria accompanied by frothy urine and orthopnea. The patient had previously undergone three sessions of hemodialysis and had received blood transfusions. Obstetric history revealed the patient to be P3A1L2 (three pregnancies, one abortion, and two living children).

Upon physical examination, the patient was found to be in a stable general condition, albeit with notable vital sign abnormalities. Her blood pressure was elevated at 170/90 mmHg, with tachycardia (110 beats per minute) and tachypnea (35 breaths per minute). The patient was febrile (101 F) with an oxygen saturation of 94% on room air. Random blood glucose was 137 mg/dL. Clinical examination revealed pallor and edema, but no icterus, clubbing, cyanosis, or lymphadenopathy. Cardiovascular and gastrointestinal examinations were unremarkable. Respiratory auscultation demonstrated bilateral basal crepitations. Neurologically, the patient was fully conscious with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15, although she reported paresthesia. Laboratory investigations revealed significant hematological and biochemical abnormalities (Table 1).

The patient's hemoglobin was markedly reduced at 5.2 g/dL, indicative of severe anemia. While the total leukocyte count (7100/mm3) and differential counts were within normal ranges, renal function tests were notably abnormal. Blood urea (109 mg/dL) and serum creatinine levels were substantially elevated (5.6 mg/dL), confirming significant renal impairment. Electrolyte analysis showed normal sodium (137 mEq/L) and slightly elevated potassium (4.8 mEq/L) levels. Liver function tests and coagulation parameters (PTI 85%) were within normal limits, and viral markers were non-reactive. Urinalysis demonstrated significant proteinuria (+++) without glycosuria, ketonuria, or pyuria. Renal ultrasonography suggested bilateral medullary disease.

A renal biopsy was considered necessary because the patient had significant renal impairment, including CKD, elevated renal function parameters (blood urea and serum creatinine), and marked proteinuria, which prompted further investigation to elucidate the underlying pathology (Figures 1, 2).
Proband first biopsy images under electron microscopy revealing numerous lamellated inclusion Zebra bodies in the glomerular visceral and tubular epithelial cells confirming Fabry disease.
Renal electron microscopy images taken from the probands' second biopsy. Zebra bodies are still present.

Histopathological examination revealed widespread glomerular and segmental tuft sclerosis within the renal medulla and cortical parenchyma. Notably, the podocytes exhibited enlargement with fine vacuolization, a characteristic finding in Fabry disease (Figures 3, 4).

Histopathological findings confirming diffuse fine vacuolization and remarkable cytoplasmic expansion of visceral epithelial cells/podocytes (stained with H&E, periodic acid Schiff (PAS), silver methenamine, Masson's trichrome (MT), and Congo red)
Direct immunofluorescence image showing renal medulla and cortical parenchymal area containing many globally sclerosed glomeruli.

However, no evidence of crescent formation, tuft necrosis, intracapillary thrombi, or congophilic deposits in the visualized glomeruli was noted. These histological features, combined with the clinical presentation and biochemical profile, led to a definitive diagnosis of Fabry disease. The patient's management involved sequential hemodialysis and diuretic therapy. To control hypertension, the patient was started on enalapril at a dose of 5 mg twice daily, with a target range of 5-40 mg per day. Follow-up was scheduled every four to six weeks to monitor blood pressure, renal function (estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), creatinine), and proteinuria. The patient was ultimately discharged in satisfactory condition on a regimen of maintenance hemodialysis.
Discussion

In females, the onset of Fabry disease symptoms mirrors that in males, but with a lower prevalence at any given age. Heterozygous females can experience a range of symptoms, including acroparesthesias, angiokeratomas, hypohidrosis, cornea verticillata, chronic abdominal pain, and diarrhea. With age, they may develop cardiac issues (fibrosis, left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), arrhythmias, valvular disease), cerebrovascular events (transient ischemic attacks (TIAs), strokes), and, less frequently, kidney problems (proteinuria, CKD). When CKD occurs, the progression to end-stage kidney disease is similar in males. Cardiac, cerebrovascular, and kidney diseases generally appear a decade later than in males. A Fabry Registry study of 1,077 females found that 70% reported symptoms, with a median onset age of 13 years, and 20% experienced major events by a median age of 46 years.

The present rare case of lysosomal storage disorder explains the multisystemic manifestations observed in the female patient, including renal dysfunction, hypertension, and neurological symptoms. Current guidelines recommend screening for Fabry disease in patients exhibiting at least two of the following clinical features: reduced sweating (anhidrosis or hypohidrosis), angiokeratomas (a characteristic reddish-purple skin rash localized to the bathing trunk area), or a personal and/or family history of renal failure. Furthermore, a history of acroparesthesias, characterized by burning or hot pain in the extremities, particularly during febrile episodes, or a history of exercise, heat, or cold intolerance, should prompt further investigation. Diagnostic evaluation is also warranted in individuals with sporadic or non-autosomal dominant patterns of unexplained cardiac hypertrophy, especially in the absence of male-to-male transmission.

Microscopic urinalysis can reveal mulberry bodies in the sediments, which are distal epithelial cells with accumulated globotriaosylceramide exhibiting a characteristic whorl-like appearance. Renal biopsy may demonstrate the Maltese cross pattern due to the birefringence of lipid droplets, primarily consisting of cholesterol esters. Treatment strategies for Fabry disease encompass a multifaceted approach, including anticoagulation and enzyme replacement therapies, such as agalsidase beta and pegunigalsidase alfa. Recent advancements have introduced oral chaperone therapy (migalastat) as an additional treatment option. Patient management involves sequential hemodialysis and diuretic therapy. This case underscores the importance of a high index of suspicion for Fabry disease in patients presenting with multisystem involvement, particularly renal dysfunction, to ensure timely diagnosis and appropriate management.
Conclusions

The present case illustrates the significance of recognizing Fabry disease in female patients, highlighting the need for heightened clinical awareness. The patient's presentation with multisystem involvement, including renal dysfunction and neurological symptoms, underscores the complexity of diagnosing Fabry disease in females who can exhibit a wide spectrum of clinical manifestations. Early diagnosis is crucial to initiate appropriate treatments, such as enzyme replacement and oral chaperone therapies, to mitigate disease progression and improve patient outcomes. This case emphasizes the importance of a comprehensive approach to diagnosing and managing Fabry disease, even in populations traditionally considered at lower risk.

passages.text: Reducing Energy Costs during Hydrogen Production from Water Electrolysis by Coupling Small Molecule Oxidation: From Molecular Catalysis to Industrial Exploration

Hydrogen energy has garnered significant attention in recent years as a solution to address the global energy crisis and environmental pollution. While water electrolysis stands out as the most promising method to produce green hydrogen, the sluggish reaction kinetics of the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) on the anode increases the cost of hydrogen production. One potential solution to this challenge is replace OER with the thermodynamically more favorable oxidation of small molecules, which can efficiently reduce the energy cost while simultaneously yielding high-value chemicals. Up to now, various organic oxidation reactions have been reported to couple with hydrogen evolution, including alcohol oxidation, biomass platform molecule upgrading, and sacrificial reagents oxidation associated with wastewater treatments. This review concentrates on the recent advancements in the mechanism, catalyst, reactor, and process in this field, with a discussion on its prospects for commercialization.
Introduction

With the continuous consumption of fossil resources and the increasing global environmental pollution, the search for clean and renewable energy has become the common goal of all countries in the world.- Hydrogen, as a zero carbon-content substance, is regarded as an important carrier for global energy storage and transportation. Many countries have made short- or long-term plans for the development of the hydrogen energy industry. At present, reforming limited fossil resources such as coal and natural gas is still the dominant route to produce hydrogen, but the massive CO2 emission is against the original intention of green development. Besides, the impurity CO could bring troubles to the downstream units of hydrogen utilization, especially the catalyst poison in fuel cells. Water electrolysis that uses water as the only raw material and renewable electricity as the driving force, has become a perspective way to produce hydrogen sustainably.- In over water splitting (OWS), the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) are the two half reactions occurring at the cathode and anode, respectively. However, the oxidation of water or OH- is difficult and a high equilibrium potential of 1.23 V vs RHE is required by the OER side. Since four electrons are transferred during the generation of one oxygen molecule, the actual potential at industrial current density is even higher due to its sluggish kinetics. Apart from this, O2 can permeate through the diaphragm to the cathode and thus mix with H2, which would cause a safety hazard.- Therefore, replacing the OER reaction with the oxidation of small molecules has attracted great attention, as its theoretical potential is usually significantly lower than that of OER.-

To enhance both energy and mass utilization, several factors must be addressed. First, considering thermodynamics, organic oxidation tends to occur more readily than water oxidation. Therefore, achieving a low potential in organic oxidation at low current densities (for example, 10 mA cm-2) is feasible. However, at the industrial current density of 0.5-2 A cm-2, the overpotential of organic oxidation may surpass that of the OER due to the complexity of oxidation process, leading to increased energy consumption. Hence, there is an urgent need to develop electrocatalysts with high activity and selectivity to reduce electrolysis potential and suppress competitive OER. Second, the organic substrates should ideally exhibit good solubility in water to ensure adequate conductivity and the presence of sufficiently active oxygen species at high current density. Lastly, for large-scale hydrogen evolution, the organic substrates should be economically viable and readily available. Depending on the desired products, the alternative oxidation reactions that meet the aforementioned criteria can be categorized into two groups. One involves upgrading substrates such as alcohol, aldehydes, and amines into high-value-added products, thereby promoting the hydrogen economy through energy savings and increased utilization. The other employs sacrificial agents derived from waste or pollutant streams on the anodic side, where reactants are oxidized into inert but low-value products like CO2, H2O, N2, etc.- This review provides an overview of recent advancements in the electrooxidation reactions mentioned above, focusing on the electrochemical reaction mechanism, electrocatalysts, reactor design, and product separations. In addition, the problems and challenges toward industrial application of coupling hydrogen evolution with organic oxidation are discussed.
Organic/Inorganic Electrooxidation System
Alcohol Oxidation

Compared with OER, alcohol oxidation reactions (AOR) exhibit faster reaction kinetics and a lower theoretical oxidation potential, attracting significant attention in recent years. According to reports, various AORs can be integrated with water electrolysis to produce hydrogen, thereby reducing the electrolytic voltage and simultaneously yielding aldehydes, acids, and other high-value-added chemicals.
Methanol

Methanol, being the smallest alcohol molecule, can undergo selective oxidation to produce formic acid, an essential intermediate in crucial chemical industry commonly used in the synthesis of numerous fine chemicals.- The global production capacity of methanol has exceeded 179 million tons, and producing formic acid (537 $ per ton) from methanol (373 $ per ton) can increase the value by 164 $ per ton. The anodic reaction can be illustrated as follows:

Xiang et al. used a carbon paper-supported Pt-Co3O4 electrocatalyst (Pt-Co3O4/CP) as a bifunctional electrocatalyst for both HER and methanol oxidation, and found that only a cell voltage of 0.555 V is required to achieve a current density of 10 mA cm-2 under alkaline conditions with 2.0 M methanol, which is 1.022 V lower than that of OWS. The anodic Faraday efficiency (FE) of formic acid is higher than 90%, and the cathodic FE of hydrogen is close to 100% (Figure 1b, c). However, the use of noble metals not only elevates the cost of hydrogen production, but is also subject to the poison by CO generated during reaction. Hao et al. prepared Ni(OH)2 nanoarrays on nickel foam through hydrothermal synthesis. During electrolysis, Ni(OH)2 is further oxidized into NiOOH, forming the active sites for the oxidation of methanol, and a current density of 100 mA cm-2 was achieved at 1.36 V under alkaline conditions (Figure 1d-f). Density functional theory (DFT) showed that HCOOH had the smallest Gibbs free energy at the catalyst surface compared to a series of reaction intermediates, and the further oxidation of HCOOH to CO2 required overcoming a high energy barrier (0.88 eV), which hindered the further oxidation of formic acid. In a diaphragm-free electrolyzer, formic acid was the only product at the anode while the hydrogen FE at the cathode was higher than 92%.

To promote the activity at large current density, Zhao et al. reported a defect-rich Ni3S2-CNFS nanoheterostructures catalyst, on which the oxidation potential decreased to 1.40 V vs RHE at a current density of 100 mA cm-2 in 1.0 M methanol. Meanwhile, the anodic reaction current density reached 1000 mA cm-2 at 1.74 V vs. RHE, which was much lower than that of OER (Figure 2a-c). It is shown that the in situ formed NiOOH and SOx has a synergistic effect to regulate the d-band center of Ni3S2, which facilitates the conversion of methanol to formate while inhibits the further oxidation of methanol to CO2. Ghosh et al. compared the catalytic activity of nickel phosphide in different phases for methanol oxidation (Figure 2d-f), among which Ni12P5 exhibits excellent activity of 210 mA cm-2 at 1.72 V vs RHE in methanol oxidation. It was found that Ni12P5 was activated by the formation of a thinner oxidized Ni layer (Ni(OH)2/NiOOH), which provides ample adsorption sites for OH- groups and bidentate adsorption sites for the carboxylated products, thereby further inhibiting the oxidation of carboxylic groups to CO2.

Ethanol

Ethanol, derived from renewable biomass, yields lower-value oxidation products such as acetic acid (or ethyl acetate) and formic acid. However, its oxidation intermediates are less toxic to the catalysts compared to methanol, especially on noble metals. Consequently, substituting OER with ethanol oxidation can enhance the activity and stability of the catalysts. Sheng et al. accelerated the kinetics of ethanol oxidation by phosphorylating CoS2 (Co-S-P/CC, Figure 3a, b), which greatly improved the charge transfer process of the catalyst, and the P treatment also reduced the adsorption free energy of atomic hydrogen at the metal sites, so that Co-S-P/CC exhibited excellent EOR and HER catalytic activities. When Co-S-P/CC was used as a bifunctional catalyst for the simultaneous ethanol oxidation and water electrolysis, a current density of 10 mA cm-2 was achieved at a voltage of only 1.63 V vs RHE. After 10 h of electrolysis, the FE of acetic acid was 67.2%, and the cathodic product was high-purity hydrogen (Figure 3c, d). Yin et al. utilized 1 nm PtIr nanowires (NWs) as bifunctional catalysts for the oxidation of ethanol coupled with HER under acidic conditions. A reported lowest voltage of 0.61 V vs RHE to reach the current density of 10 mA cm-2 was obtained on PtIr, which is much lower than those of Pt NWs (0.85 V) and commercial Pt/C (0.86 V), and can have the highest FE of 85% for 1,1-diethoxyethane (DEE) production and 94.0% for hydrogen evolution among all the reported electrosynthesis catalysts. In situ infrared tests showed that the PtIr NWs could promote the activation of O-H and C-H bonds in ethanol, thus facilitating the formation of acetaldehyde intermediates, which were further oxidized to DEE under the catalysis of sulfuric acid (Figure 3e-h).

Ethylene Glycol

The oxidation of ethylene glycol (EG), the smallest diol molecule, has the potential to replace OER. However, the EG oxidation reaction (EGOR) is more complex compared to methanol and ethanol oxidation, yielding numerous products. These include C2 products such as glycolaldehyde, glycolic acid, glyoxylic acid, and adipic acid, as well as C1 products like formic acid and carbon dioxide. Market research results reveal that the industrial price of EG with excess capacity is only 642 $ per ton, and the prices of its oxidation products, glycolaldehyde, glyoxal, glycolic acid (GLYA), and glyoxalic acid (GA), are 928 $ per ton, 1486 $ per ton, 2143 $ per ton, and 3457 $ per ton, respectively. Meanwhile the C1 product, FA, has an industrial price of 537 $ per ton. Therefore, through oxidizing EG, a range of high value-added chemicals can be obtained. When using noble metal (Pt, Pd, etc.) catalysts, EGOR can occur at voltages lower than 1.0 V vs. RHE. However, CO and CO-like intermediates tend to be adsorbed the active surface, poisoning the active sites of noble metals and hindering the long-term operation of EGOR. To address this issue, it is necessary to regulate the adsorption energy of the poisoning intermediate on the metal surface. Si et al. reported a PdAg alloy catalyst for EGOR to obtain high value-added ethanoic acid by weakening the adsorption of O=*CCH2OH at the Pd active site through intermetallic charge transfer, thus prolonging the lifetime of Pd sites (Figure 4a-d). Liu et al. loaded Pd on NF to prepare Pd-Ni(OH)2 catalysts, which achieved electrocatalytic stability up to 200 h, by promoting the adsorption of OH to inhibit the poisoning from aldehyde intermediates. And the overall yield of GLYA from PET could reach 58.5% after hydrolysis and electrochemical oxidation (Figure 4e). Yan et al. electrodeposited Au/Ni(OH)2 catalytic material with high EGOR activity, and also carried out a sequential electrooxidation reaction with EG obtained from 70 g of PET, which ultimately yielded 13.7 g of GLYA and 9.4 L of H2 (Figure 4f). Nevertheless, the problem of noble metal-based poisoning is still not completely solved. However, non-noble metals such as Ni are also widely used in catalytic EG oxidation, and indirect oxidation strategies are employed to solve the poisoning problem of noble metal catalysts. Li et al. synthesized NiSe2 with different morphology and crystallographic phases, and found their catalytic performance in EG oxidation is significantly different. The branched NiSe2 nanoparticles displayed the best performance, with a current density of up to 95 mA cm-2 in an electrolyte containing 1 M KOH and 1 M EG, owing to the improved surface coverage, active species diffusion and electrochemical surface area (ECSA). The FE of formic acid is also high up to 80%, with FE of hydrogen close to 100% (Figure 4g, h). DFT calculation revealed that glycolate is the most important intermediate during EGOR, where the C-C bond is broken to be electro-oxidized to formate, or it is maintained to be electro-oxidized into oxalate.

Glycerol

Glycerol (GE) is primarily obtained through hydrolysis of epichlorohydrin derived from the chlorination of propylene or as a byproduct of biodiesel production. The oxidation of GE yields numerous oxygenated chemical intermediates, but the conventional oxidation reactions often require harsh external conditions such as high temperature, high pressure, and external feed, rendering them costly and time-consuming. In contrast, renewable energy-driven electrocatalytic GE oxidation presents an attractive approach for synthesizing valuable chemicals. The GE molecule contains two primary hydroxyl groups and one secondary hydroxyl group, leading to the production of a series of C1, C2, and C3 products upon oxidation. Consequently, modulating selectivity becomes challenging due to the similarity of the activity of the three hydroxyl groups. Currently, numerous catalysts have been investigated for the electrooxidation of GE, and various potential mechanisms for the reaction have been explored. However, owing to the diversity of catalysts and the influence of reaction conditions (e.g., pH, potential, temperature, etc.), the mechanism of GEOR remains uncertain.

Noble metals, predominantly Pt, Pd, and Au, have a propensity to adsorb GE and active intermediates on their surfaces, and exhibit excellent catalytic activity. Research indicates that the deprotonation of hydroxyl groups is the initial step in GE oxidation. Due to its lower d-band center (-2.25 eV), Pt exhibits high efficiency in GE deprotonation, thereby displaying superior catalytic activity. However, the first step of EG oxidation on a single noble metal electrode typically involves dehydrogenation of primary hydroxyl groups, promoting the formation of glyceraldehyde and glyceric acid (GLA), among others. The selectivity of the oxidized products is closely linked to pH and electrolysis potential: lower pH levels correspond to lower catalytic activity in GEOR, while an increase in electrolysis voltage gradually shifts oxidized products from C3 to C2 and C1 products. To address issues related to CO poisoning and regulate the product selectivity, modifications such as micromorphology modification, alloying, and substrate design are employed to modify the noble metal catalysts. Anil et al. compared mesoporous Pt catalysts with different pore sizes and structures, and the one with hierarchical pore had the highest GEOR activity, where large pores enable rapid diffusion and small pores provide larger specific surface area, and the main products were GLA and oxalic acid (OA). Matheus et al. and Michael et al. introduced a Bi promoter into Pt/C, and Pt-Bi provided dual active sites for sec-hydroxyl oxidation, enhancing the catalytic activity of Pt by about 5-fold (Figure 5a), hindered the formation of toxic intermediates such as CO, and prevented the breakage of the C-C bond, resulting in an increase in the yield of GLA (Figure 5b,c). Yan et al. designed a synergistic catalyst to generate highly selective lactic acid (LA, 82% selectivity) at high current densities (226 mA cm-2 at 1.05 V vs RHE) by decorating BiOx nanolayers on Au particles (BiOx/Au). Similar effect has also been reported by the introduction of Sb element. Li et al. alloyed Pt with Au (hp-PtAu/NF), which altered the adsorption structure of GE on the catalyst surface and similarly inhibited C-C bond breaking, ensuring high GEOR activity (921.5 mA cm-2 at 1.6 V vs RHE) and high C3 selectivity (95%). However, under the catalysis of noble metals, high-value products can only be obtained at lower potentials because GE is susceptible to be over oxidized into CO2 at higher potentials. Therefore, transition metal-based catalysts such as Ni, Co, and Cu are more attractive from an economic point of view. Mohamed et al. increased the catalytic activity of Ni for GEOR by investigating on nickel electrode surface in a sinusoidal wave treatment in a solution of 0.1 M Na2SO4 + 30 mM ascorbic acid, which roughened the electrode surface along with the formation of nickel hydroxide, thus increasing the current density by more than nine times, reducing the onset potential by 45 mV, and obtaining GE aldehydes as main product. Vo et al. reported the generation of dihydroxyacetone (DHA) from the oxidation of the sec-hydroxyl group on amorphous CoOx with ~60% selectivity, where CoOOH acts as an active site and promotes deprotonation of the hydroxyl group on the sec-carbon.

Aromatic Alcohols

Benzyl alcohol (BA) is a commonly used aromatic alcohol for anodic oxidation. Similar to the oxidation of fatty alcohols, BA undergoes initial oxidation to form benzaldehyde, which is then further oxidized to benzoic acid. Due to the ease of adsorption and oxidation of aldehydes into acids, the dominant product of BA oxidation typically consists of the less valuable benzoic acid. Huang et al. used amorphous Co-NiOOH nanosheets to catalyze BA oxidation, which could reach industrial-scale current density of more than 400 mA cm-2, with 99% yield of benzoic acid under only 15 min of electrolysis in a highly concentrated BA solution (up to 0.1 M) (Figure 6a-c). Li et al. also reported an Au/CoOOH catalyst with gold nanoparticles supported on cobalt oxide nanosheets for the oxidation of BA, and the EGORllHER system achieved 4.8 A current at 2.0 V voltage in 1 M KOH. To deal with the catalyst deactivation during alcohol electrooxidation, Li et al. proposed an intermittent electrolysis strategy to refresh the metal sites by utilizing the reducing properties of alcohols themselves, so that prolonged alcohol electrolysis can be achieve (Figure 6d-f). In recent years, how to improve aldehydes selectivity has attracted increasing attention. One strategy is to use radical trappers such as 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidin-1-oxo (TEMPO) to capture aldehydes and avoid its further oxidation into acids. Wang et al. reported the catalytic oxidation of BA on h-Ni(OH)2 prepared by the etching of NiZn(OH)2. The catalyst contains a large number of holes and oxygen vacancies, which provides high exposed surface area and abundant active sites, and the oxygen vacancies increases the charge transfer between VO-Ni(OH)2 and BA. Without TEMPO, the selectivity to benzoic acid is above 92% at BA conversion of 99%. After TEMPO is introduced, the selectivity to benzaldehyde was promoted to 94% at 90% conversion. In the same group, Zheng et al. constructed layered structures to expose more active sites of NC@CuCo2NX/CF, and the synergistic effect of Cu-N and Co-N compounds adjusted the adsorption strength of reactive oxygen species, thus accelerated the reaction kinetics. In the oxidation of BA assisted by TEMPO, high selectivity (>95%) of benzaldehyde was also obtained.

From previous studies, it is not difficult to discover that alcohols tend to be oxidized to acids under alkaline conditions. Although the addition of TEMPO can lead to highly selective benzaldehyde products, the introduction of TEMPO is not the optimal solution, and it is crucial to probe deeply into the mechanism of benzaldehyde oxidation reaction and to regulate the degree of BA oxidation. Xu et al. proposed a strategy to control the extent of BA oxidation by regulating the local microenvironment of NiO. It was revealed that during the electrooxidation of alcohols, the hydroxyl groups of alcohols are first dehydrogenated to form radical intermediates, then the intermediates are further oxidized rapidly to form the corresponding aldehydes. The reversible hydration of aldehydes forms the gem-diol intermediates, which then generate the corresponding acids (Figure 7a). Therefore, how to inhibit the hydration reaction of aldehydes becomes the key to synthesize aldehyde compounds. Using K2CO3 as the electrolyte, Xu et al. succeeded in obtaining 100% selectivity for benzaldehyde through the salting-out effect, which inhibited the interaction of aldehyde intermediates with water while decreasing the electrolyte concentration, resulting in the concentration of organic molecules to be precipitated at the electrode/electrolyte interface (Figure 7b-d). Meanwhile, this method can also be applied to the electrooxidation of other alcohols or aldehydes, or even other functional groups.

Biomass Platform Molecules

Biomass is among the most abundant and renewable carbon resources globally, capable of being converted into fuels and chemicals typically derived from coals and oils. Biomass platform molecules are fundamental substances obtained through the biological and chemical conversion of biomass hydrocarbons, including cellulose, starch, lignin, etc. Featuring various active groups within their molecule structure, the biomass platform molecules can be converted into many high-value chemicals and materials. Notably, the feasibility of coupling furfural (FUR) oxidation to 2-furoic acid, or 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF) oxidation to 2,5-furandicarboxylic acid with HER has been extensively explored.
Furfural

2-Furoic acid finds common application as a raw material in both the pharmaceutical and plastics industries, typically obtained by oxidizing FUR. However, in solutions with high alkali concentration, FUR is susceptible to Cannizzaro disproportionation, resulting in a theoretical acid yield of only 50% and consequently low raw material utilization. Directly oxidation FUR to 2-furoic acid using water as the sole oxygen source, propelled by electrical energy, presents a viable means to enhance resource utilization and holds promising applications. A series of researches on aldehydes have been carried out through alloys, oxides, hydroxides, phosphates, sulfides, etc. Zhang et al. synthesized Ni2P/CFC using gas-phase hydrothermal method. The high-valence Ni species formed during electrocatalysis exhibited higher furfural oxidation reaction (FOR) activity compared to Cu3P/CFC, with 2-furoic acid selectivity close to 100%, and HER FE between 90.0% ~ 98.0% in the applied potential range of 1.2 to 1.7 V vs RHE (Figure 8a-c). However, most research only compared the activity between FUR oxidation and OER in small current density (10-300 mA cm-2). With the increasing of potential, the FUR oxidation would become slower than OER, leading to the acceleration of competitive oxygen evolution during electrolysis, probably because of the larger molecule size of FUR that covers more active sites and the multiple electron transfer steps. To improve the catalytic activity of FOR and inhibit the OER at industrial current density, Zeng et al. reported a NiMoP/NF obtained by sequential reduction and phosphorylation of hydrothermally synthesized NiMoO4/NF precursor. It achieved 500 mA cm-2 with only 1.46 V vs RHE in FUR solution, significantly better than the OER activity over commercial RuO2/NF under the same current density (1.57 V vs RHE) The selectivity and FE of 2-furoic acid also reached 99.2% and 96.7%, respectively (Figure 8d-g). DFT calculation indicated that the good OER activity over RuO2 is attributed to the moderate adsorption energy of *O, *OH, and *OOH, while NiMoP can spontaneously adsorb *O and *OH, but the energy barrier from O* to *OOH was too high, thus the oxygen evolution was blocked while the FUR oxidation was promoted.

5-Hydroxymethylfurfural

5-Hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF), as another biomass-derived platform molecule, can be oxidized into a variety of valuable chemicals due to the presence of hydroxymethyl and formyl groups on the furan ring. These include 2,5-diformylfuran (DFF), 5-hydroxymethyl-2-furancarboxylic acid (HMFCA), 5-formyl-2-furancarboxylic acid (FFCA), and 2,5-furandicarboxylic acid (FDCA). Notably, FDCA is a biobased aromatic compound used in the synthesis of various derivatives, particularly polyethylene furanoate, which serves as an alternative material to the widely used polyethylene terephthalate (PET). Compared with the traditional thermocatalytic method that requires high temperature, pressure, and precious metal catalysts, transition metal-catalyzed HMF electrooxidation to produce FDCA is more aligned with the principles of green production. The possible pathways of HMF oxidation reaction are shown in Figure 9, including hydroxyl-preferential oxidation to produce the DFF intermediate and aldehyde-preferential oxidation to produce the HMFCA intermediate, both of which are further oxidized to FFCA and the final product FDCA. Cha et al. pointed out that the current distribution did not change significantly with the addition of HMF when TEMPO was not added in 0.5 M borate buffer solution (PBS, pH = 9.2), with Au as the electrode and OER as the main competing reaction. With the introduction of TEMPO, it produces TEMPO+ in lower potential oxidation, but HMF oxidation is thermodynamically more favorable than TEMPO oxidation, so TEMPO as a mediator and catalyst can be used to achieve low-potential HMF oxidation without competing with water oxidation, to obtain yields >99% and FE > 93%. Zhou et al. compared the reaction route of HMF oxidation to FDCA using DFT (Figure 10a), and fond the potential change from HMF to HMFCA was -0.165 V vs SHE, lower than that from HMF to DFF (-0.048 V vs. SHE). In situ IR and product detection results indicated the oxidation intermediate was HMFCA (Figure 10b,c). Indeed, the oxidation of aldehyde groups is easily inhibited in neutral media. Therefore, Ge et al. conducted related research and found that the oxidation of HMF was affected by the pH value of the electrolyte, with neutral media more favorable for aldehyde formation than alkaline media. Thus, hydroxyl oxidation is the most effective pathway for HMF oxidation in 1.0 M PBS, with DFF being the major intermediate. In the presence of Ru1-NiO catalyst, the DFF selectivity reaches 90% and the FE reaches about 70% at 1.5 V. The DFF selectivity is also shown to be higher than that of the FFCA. Up to 75.8% FFCA yield could be obtained by further oxidation. On the contrary, just by changing the pH of the electrolyte, the HMF oxidation product distribution changes dramatically and the final product becomes FDCA (Figure 11). Xu et al. used a two-step electrodeposition strategy to load single-atom Ru onto NiFe-LDH (Ru0.3/NiFe) for HMFOR. The introduction of Ru leads to the expansion of the LDH crystal and changes its electronic structure. Theoretical calculations revealed that a surface charge transfer occurs around the Ru atom, and the Ru sites in low-coordination state are optimal sites for OH adsorption and proton capture from HMF. As a result, excellent electrocatalytic performance in HMFOR was demonstrated, resulting in a very low overpotential (243 mV at 10 mA cm-2), 99.43% HMF conversion, 99.24% FDCA selectivity and 98.68% yield in 1 M KOH with 7.5 mmol L-1.

Sacrificial Reagent Oxidation

With the advancement of human civilization, vast quantities of industrial and domestic wastewater are generated, decomposing very slowly in nature and posing potential harm to human health if left untreated.- Conversely, certain pollutants such as ammonia, hydrazine, urea, etc. can be oxidized on anode at lower voltage than OER, resulting in the release of only CO2, H2O, and N2. Therefore, these pollutants can act as sacrificial reagents for anodic oxidation reaction to couple with HER, effectively addressing environmental pollution while decreasing energy cost during hydrogen production simultaneously.
Hydrazine

Hydrazine is widely used as an industrial raw material for rocket fuel, battery fuel, and agricultural and pharmaceutical products. However, its untreated emission poses significant environmental pollution risks to human life. In order to reduce the voltage required for water electrolysis and realize energy-efficient hydrogen production, a novel water decomposition electrochemical system called hydrazine-assisted HER (HERllHzOR) was established by using the half-reaction hydrazine oxidation reaction (HzOR) instead of OER. Compared to other AOR, HzOR offers several advantages: (i) the theoretical oxidation potential of hydrazine is merely 0.33 V vs. RHE, resulting in a cell voltage typically below 1.0 V for HERllHzOR; (ii) the products of HzOR are nitrogen and water, which improves the safety of the reaction and avoids CO2 emission; (iii) the absence of carbon participation in the reaction prevents the catalyst poisoning by CO during the process. Most reports on hydrazine-assisted hydrogen production are conducted in alkaline medium, involving two half-reactions and the total reaction as follows:

HzOR, as a four-electron reaction, still requires an efficient and stable catalyst to be oxidized. Nickel and cobalt based materials are currently used in most reported hydrazine assisted HER bifunctional electrocatalysts. For the first time, Sun's team utilized N2P nanoarrays grown on NF for a HERllHzOR system, which requires only 1.0 V of cell voltage to input 500 mA cm-2 in a solution of 1 M KOH with 0.5 M hydrazine. The electrolysis maintained stable for 10 h at 100 mA cm-2 with 100% HER FE. In the HERllOER system, an output of 20 mA cm-2 required a voltage of up to 1.6 V. Cobalt based materials, especially cobalt phosphide and cobalt sulfide, are also used in HERllHzOR systems due to their excellent conductivity and activity. Wang et al. used a simple hydrothermal method combined with an annealing process to anchor CoP on Ti mesh (CoP/TiM) for hydrazine-assisted hydrogen production. When the hydrazine concentration is increased to 0.1 M, only 6 mV of potential is required to drive 100 mA cm-2, which is superior to the noble metal Pt/C/TiM. For HERllHzOR reactions with large number of bubbles, it is essential to ensure rapid penetration of the electrolyte to the electrode interface and desorption of bubbles to improve the reaction kinetics. Zhao et al. used a sacrificial template method via pulse electrodeposition and dealloying process, in which nickel and copper from the corresponding metal salt were first codeposited onto the surface of NF, then copper was selectively dissolved to obtain the Ni(Cu)/NF catalyst (Figure 12a, b). The prepared catalyst presented a hierarchically porous structure with a large specific surface area. In 1 M KOH with 0.5 M hydrazine solutions, the HERllHzOR system requires only a cell voltage of 0.41 V to obtain 100 mA cm-2. Later, the same group synthesized a double-layer copper doped nickel cubic nanopore (Ni(Cu)CNP) catalyst and a NiFeP catalyst (Ni(Cu)@NiFeP/NM) coated with Ni(Cu) alloy nanotubes on a nickel mesh (NM) for the HERllHzOR system (Figure 12c, d). Ni(Cu)CNP exhibits a hollow cubic structure, and 100 mA cm-2 can be achieved in a hydrazine-assisted hydrogen production system with a cell voltage of 0.34 V. Similarly, Ni(Cu)@NiFeP/NM requires a cell voltage of only 0.49 V to obtain 100 mA cm-2. In short, the hierarchical porous structure exhibits the best electrochemical activity and electrolytic efficiency in the HERllHzOR system (Figure 12e).

Urea

Urea serves as not only an important chemical product but also the primary component (~0.3 mol L-1) in the urine produced in large quantities in human and animal life. If discharged directly into nature without treatment, then it undergoes decomposition into ammonia under light conditions, evolving into environmental pollutants such as nitrogen oxides and nitrites, thereby causing serious harm to the environment. Therefore, finding effective methods for treating urea-rich wastewater is crucial for mitigating energy crises and environmental issues. Compared to traditional methods, the coupled assisted hydrogen production by urea oxidation reaction (UOR) offers advantages such as low theoretical thermodynamic voltage (0.37 V vs RHE) and nontoxic products. The reaction equation of urea in alkaline medium is as follows:

As observed, the UOR involves a 6-electron transfer process characterized by slow reaction kinetics. While noble metal catalysts are typically employed as general-purpose catalysts for UOR, their scarcity and high cost restrict their widespread application. Therefore, researchers are now directing their attention toward transition metal-based catalysts, mainly nickel-based catalysts, owing to their relatively superior performance in UOR.

Boote's team confirmed through in situ characterization that NiOOH is the active site for urea oxidation. According to the electrochemical chemical (E-C) mechanism, Ni(II) is first electrochemically oxidized to Ni(III), then the adsorbed urea molecule is oxidized by the Ni(III) intermediate. The specific reaction is as follows:

In another possible direct oxidation mechanism, the urea molecule initially adsorbed onto NiOOH active sites via bridge coordination. Subsequently, it reacts with OH- in the bulk solution to yield CO2 and N2. Regardless of the catalytic oxidation pathways, the desorption of CO2 is characterized by the highest free energy and is regarded as the rate-determining step.

The rational design of the electronic structure of the catalyst is essential to realize the UOR at high current density, such as alloying, amorphization, doping, defect engineering, and construction of heterojunction structure. Alloying metals with other elements can optimize the electron distribution and facilitate the adsorption/desorption behavior of intermediates, thus accelerating the UOR kinetics. Zhang et al. synthesized metastable Cu0.5Ni0.5 alloy via a one-step electrodeposition process. Due to the phase segregation of Cu0.5Ni0.5 during the UOR process, the NiOOH active phase can be generated rapidly leading to high UOR activity. The cell voltage of HERllUOR system was 305 mV lower than the conventional HERllOER system in obtaining 100 mA cm-2. Compared with crystalline catalysts, amorphous catalysts of the same composition could show better stability due to their structural flexibility and self-healing ability. In addition, the amorphous form can also expose abundant active sites and change the local environment around the active species, which in turn changes the adsorption of the reactants to enhance the catalytic activity. Chen's team synthesized Ni(OH)2 nanosheet-supported amorphous Ni sulfoselenide catalysts on nickel foam (Ni-S-Se/NF) using hydrothermal and etching processes (Figure 14a). The amorphous hydroxyl oxides formed in situ during UOR resulted in the rapid formation of NiOOH. Therefore, only a cell voltage of 1.47 V is required to obtain 10 mA cm-2 in the HERllUOR system. Doping heteroatoms in the lattice disrupts the long-range ordering of atoms, thus disturbs the electron distribution, changes the interfacial wettability, and exposes more active sites, all of which can enhance the electrocatalytic performance. Electron-rich metal heteroatoms can not only improve the electrical conductivity of catalysts, but also optimize the DeltaGH* by changing the local electronic structure. Li et al. synthesized Co and N double-doped in hcp phase metal Ni (hcp-CoNi-N/C) using N-doping induced phase transfer strategy. The double doping formed an interface favorable for urea molecule adsorption and C-N bond breaking, and improved the mass transfer by tuning the wettability of the catalyst surface (Figure 14b, c). Only 1.31 V voltage is required to obtain 10 mA cm-2, with 63 h of continuous stability in a solution with 1 M KOH and 0.33 M urea.
