Ammonia

Ammonia (NH3) is widely produced and utilized, yet without proper treatment, it can lead to gas and liquid pollution, primarily originating from domestic sewage and fertilizer industries. When released into water, it can induce eutrophication, while as gaseous pollutants, it may contribute to respiratory diseases. Similar to hydrazine, ammonia is small molecule devoid of carbon and readily susceptible to oxidation. Theoretically, the electrolysis of NH3 to produce N2 and H2 only requires a cell voltage of 0.06 V, significantly lower than water electrolysis (1.23 V). Therefore, coupling HER with ammonia oxidation reaction (AmOR) is deemed a promising technology for ammonia removal and regenerative hydrogen production. The AmOR process involves 6-electron transfer mechanism with slow kinetics, and two possible reaction pathways have been proposed:

Pt-based materials serve as highly active catalysts for AmOR; however, their limited availability and high cost hinder widespread adoption. In response, alternative transition metal catalysts have been were proposed, with nickel-based materials emerging as the most prevalent among them for AmOR applications. However, the adsorption of N-containing species via Ni-N is too strong, making the desorption of intermediates and products difficult and thus hindering the reaction kinetics. Therefore, most of the studies since 2010 have been devoted to the modification of nickel-based catalysts by doping. Wang et al. used a two-step hydrothermal method, in which Cu2O NWs were embedded in Ni(OH)2 nanoplates in the first step and CuO was covered on the surface (Ni(OH)2-Cu2O@CuO) in the second step (Figure 16a). The new silk plate nanostructures of Ni(OH)2, Cu2O, and CuO in close contact formed the dual interfaces of Ni(OH)2-Cu2O and Cu2O@CuO, which effectively protects Cu2O from oxidation, inhibits copper dissolution in the electrolyte, and promotes stability and activity toward AmOR (Figure 16b-d). It should be noticed that Cu is not an active site, and the AmOR activity will be hindered once Cu is doped in high amount.

While some of the thermodynamically favorable options for wastewater anode treatment described above exhibit clear advantages when combination with HER, there are several barriers to the practical application. First, contaminants in actual wastewater are typically present in low concentrations and accomplished by other impurities. The process of gathering, enriching, and purifying these consumptions requires additional energy consumption. Second, most of the electrooxidation processes are conducted in alkaline medium, and the addition of alkalis or salts can lead to secondary contamination of water. Besides, the presence of inorganic and organic impurities in real wastewaters may result in poisoning of the catalysts and fouling of the membranes. While it is true that substances with high purity and concentration can be produced via mature chemical processes on a large scale, such commercial feedstock would undoubtedly increase the cost of hydrogen production. Therefore, further investigation is needed to explore methods for obtaining cheap and abundant sacrificial agents to couple with HER for energy-saving purposes.

The basic characteristics of the electrooxidation reaction systems mentioned above are compared in Table 2. The advantage of alcohol oxidation is that its market is generally mature and extensive. On the contrary, the current market for FAC and FDCA is very small, but it is expected to grow significantly in the future with the development of downstream products such as polyester. For the sacrificial reagent oxidation, the products are usually emitted as exhaust and can only be economical when coupled with wastewater treatment.

Others

In addition to the organic compounds mentioned above, there are other small molecules (e.g., glucose, amines, sulfides, methane etc.) whose oxidation reactions have the potential to replace OER. As a widely available and inexpensive compound, glucose can be easily oxidized to generate high-value-added compounds such as gluconic acid (GNA) and glucosinolates (GRA). Liu et al. reported NiFeOx-NF-catalyzed electrooxidation of glucose, with a low onset potential (1.13 V vs RHE) and Tafel slope (19 mV dec-1) confirming that the electrooxidation of glucose is thermodynamically more favorable than OER. The two-electrode system for glucose oxidation-assisted hydrogen production provided a current density of 200 mA cm-2 at 1.48 V vs RHE (Figure 17a), which could be operated stably for 24 h (Figure 17b). However, Zhu et al. calculated that when glucose is electrooxidized on the Cu(OH)2 surface, the dehydrogenation of C5H11O5CHO* to C5H11O5CO* is slow, resulting in the accumulation of glucose at the electrode interface. Therefore, Zhu et al. and Xin et al. used glucose to assist Cu(I)/Cu(II) conversion with redox coupling with the HER to avoid direct oxidation of glucose on the electrode surface (Figure 17d).

The theoretical oxidation potential of primary amines (R-NH2) typically ranges from 0.5-0.8 V vs RHE, resulting in the production of valuable nitrile compounds extensively utilized in the chemical industry and pharmacy. Among these aromatic amine compounds, benzylamine stands out as the most popular choice. The synthesis of benzonitrile (BN) by electro-oxidation is more cost-effective and nonpolluting than the production of BN by the conventional ammoniation of benzoic acid. Li et al. reported a Mo0.8Ni0.2N-Ni3N heterojunction catalyst in which charge transfer leads to a shift of the d-band center of Ni, which is more favorable for the formation of NiOOH on the Ni3N surface, thus optimizing the adsorption energy of surface benzylamine. A current density of 220 mA cm-2 was achieved at 1.59 V vs RHE, and the FE of BN was as high as 99%. The BNORllHER was about 180 mV lower than the OWS at 10 mA cm-2 reaction current, and the conversion, selectivity and FE of both cathodic and anodic reactions were close to 100% (Figure 18c, e). The oxidation potential of H2S is much lower than that of the OER, but its extreme toxicity and corrosiveness cannot be ignored. Since selenides are stable in sulfur-containing solutions, Duan et al. reported a series of sulfide-resistant nickel-selenium NWs for electrocatalytic desulfurization and water electrolysis. The 100 mA cm-2 current density requires only 0.49 V vs RHE (Figure 18g), which is much lower than the potential of electrolyzed water (1.78 V vs. RHE), and the NiSe/NFllNiSe/NF membrane electrodes had an ultralow power consumption of only 2.63 kWh to produce 1 N m3 H2. The electrooxidation of methane has also attracted the interest of researchers. Tian et al. synthesized a CuOx/V2O5 composite catalyst supported on hollow porous titanium tube. The atomically dispersed CuOx and its induced Lewis acid sites facilitated the selective electrooxidation of methane into FA. The optimized catalyst achieved a FE of FA up to 92% at the current density of 14.4 mA cm-2. Further work was also reported by coupling the methane oxidation and CO2 reduction to produce FA on both cathode and anode.

Reactor Engineering and Process Development

At present, most literatures focuses on elucidating the mechanism and catalyst design, with only a few works devoted efforts to the reactor and processes for coupling organic oxidation and water splitting. water electrolysis technologies can be categorized into four classes based on ion conduction method: alkaline water electrolysis (ALKWE), proton exchange membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE), anion exchange membrane water electrolysis (AEMWE), and solid oxide electrolysis (SOEC).- Among these, ALKWE reactors are probably the most suitable devices for simultaneous organic oxidation considering the current density and catalyst stability, but their low energy efficiency hampers their future application. PEMWEs are regarded as the most promising one due to their capability to achieve high current density (2 A cm-2), produce high-purity hydrogen, and adapt well to fluctuating power source. However, due to the environment, only noble-metal or nonmetal catalysts can be used as anodic catalyst in the reaction system for assisted hydrogen production. Unfortunately, many of the organic oxidation catalysts mentioned earlier are not resistant to corrosion in PEMWEs. However, AEMWEs offer the advantages of PEMWEs and provide a base environment for stabilize non-novel metals. However, the stability of anion exchange membranes still requires improvement. SOECs operate at high temperature to reduce the input of electricity by increasing heat input, with a key challenge being how to improve ion conductivity in molten salts and interfaces. Regardless of the water electrolysis technology adopted, factors such as membrane stability and penetration in the presence of organics, the intensification of mass transfer, the mechanical and chemical durability of catalysts or electrodes, and the nonelectrochemical side reactions in electrolytes should be considered. Therefore, the rational design of electrochemical reactors is crucial for coupling hydrogen production with organic oxidations.

Many literatures have attempted to combine HER and organic oxidation in flow-cell electrolyzers to assess their performance under practical operation. According to the Nernst equation, the potential of electrode reactions can be adjusted by electrolyte pH value. Song et al, utilized an alkaline medium (pH = 14) in anode chamber and an acidic medium (pH = 0) in cathode chamber to form a mixed acid-alkaline alternative oxidation system to reduce the energy consumption in the hydrogen production process. The electrocatalytic oxidation of GLY (100 mM) in 1 M KOH with NIFe-LDH as the anode, and HER at the cathode with 20% Pt/C in 0.5 M H2SO4 were coupled. Compared with conventional water electrolysis, the hybrid EHCO system drove 500 mA cm-2 with only 1.72 V and was able to run stably for 500 h at 100 mA cm-2 (Figure 19). Li et al. synthesized Mn0.2NiS/GF catalysts for the oxidation of HMF. In a proton exchange membrane electrolyzer operated at a constant current of 5 A and a flow rate of 200 mL min-1, the cell voltage of HERllHMFOR was about 180 mV lower than the required for the HERllOER system. Similarly, Li et al. synthesized Au/CoOOH catalyst for BA oxidation in a self-made membrane electrolysis cell to evaluate its industrial potential. With a working electrode of 30 cm2, an absolute current of 4.8 A could be obtained at a potential of 2.4 V, and a BA conversion rate of 39.8 mmol h-1 and a benzoic acid production rate of 36.6 mmol h-1 were realized. However, these investigations are based on laboratory scale devices, and it is worth pondering how to solve the problems of actual industrial application scenarios.

The electrooxidation of aldehydes and ketones, biomass derivatives such as FUR and HMF, to produce a variety of high-value chemicals has been described in the previous section. These reactions are usually carried out in alkaline solutions to obtain a high current density. However, oxygen-containing functional groups are prone to non-Faraday disproportionation reaction under alkaline conditions, which is not conducive to the industrial scale-up of electrocatalytic conversion strategies for biomass derivatives. In response to the above issues, Duan's team designed a single-pass continuous flow reactor (SPCFR, Figure 18a-c). The reactor has the following characteristics: (I) High electrode area to electrolyte volume ratio to promote Faraday process; (II) Separate feeding of substrate and alkaline solution; (III) The residence time of electrolyte in the reactor is short; and (IV) The one-way conversion rate of reactants is relatively high. (II-IV) To avoid mixing of reactants/intermediates with alkali and to reduce the disproportion of substances to obtain a high-purity target product. Taking glucose electrooxidation (1 M KOH with 100 mM glucose) as an example, a one-way conversion of up to 80.2%, a selectivity of 83.8% for formate, a FE of 89.6%, and a current of 3 A at a flow rate of 1.98 mL min-1 were achieved, which were far superior to that of the intermittent reactor. By assembling nine SPCFR stacked modules, high selectivity and FE were still maintained at a current of 15 A. In addition, the device can also be used for other biomass derivative systems (Figure 20d, e).

In traditional water electrolysis process, the products are solely hydrogen or oxygen, which can be readily separated from pure water or electrolyte solution through flash separation. However, in the oxidation of organics, the separation of anodic organic products from electrolyte solution is often a complex and high-energy consuming operation, which seriously hinders industrial applications. Membrane separation technology is characterized by energy saving, high efficiency, and process simplicity, and can be integrated with electrochemical reactors. Li et al. designed a membrane reactor for the electrocatalysis oxidation of n-butanol to propionic, with a microporous Ti membrane loaded with MnO2 as anode with separation function. The reactants were permeated from the outside of the membrane to the inside, and propionic acid was obtained from the inside, thus achieving partition functionalization to improve the separation and selectivity of the products. Combining conventional chemical operation units with electrocatalysis is also a new way to achieve green environmental protection. Huang et al. used a combination of mixed electrolytic water and traditional crystallization separation process, utilizing the principle of producing weak acids from strong acids (Figure 21a). After oxidation of BA, hydrochloric acid was added to the electrolyte to achieve the conversion of benzoic acid (Ph-COOH) and potassium benzoate, resulting in high-purity white powder Ph-COOH (Figure 21b, c). Similarly, Xu et al. achieved 100% conversion of BA to benzaldehyde using the salting-out effect. It reduces the alkalinity of the electrolyte, inhibits the oxidation of aldehydes, and disrupts the hydrogen bonds between organic molecules and water by the addition of cations, leading to the aggregation of benzaldehyde at the electrolytic interface. As the concentration of benzaldehyde increases, salting out can prevent the oxidation of the aldehyde to an acid, achieve separation of the product, and regulate the selectivity of benzaldehyde.

Conclusions and Outlook

Despite the progress made so far, the industrial application of coupling water electrolysis and organic oxidation for hydrogen production is still in the early exploration stage. First, while the oxidation mechanisms of various oxidation reactions have been explored through theoretical calculations and in situ analysis in recent years, the complexity and diversity of organic oxidation render the underlying relationship between adsorption, decomposition, dehydrogenation, and oxidation uncertain. Exploring novel characterization and computation methods are urgently required to reveal the evolution of the electrode-solution interface under operating conditions. Second, although the reported oxidation catalysts exhibit good catalytic activity, industrial applications necessitate long-term durability. Thus, development of stable anodic catalyst with lifetime comparable to commercial HER catalyst is vital, and new membranes should be designed to improve the resistance to organics. Third, while most of the above reactions demonstrate good performance in small electrolyzers, their behavior in industrial electrochemical reactors with larger cell size and cell stack remains unknown, especially regarding mass transfer, gas release, heat transfer, etc. The structure and configuration of the electrochemical reactors should be optimized on the basis of pilot apparatus and combined with the mathematical model. Lastly, the polarity, high boiling point, and azeotropic nature of oxidized organics in water make its separation more challenging than that in OER, emphasizing the necessity for cointensification of reaction and separation.

In summary, recent research progress has confirmed the feasibility of water electrolysis to produce hydrogen coupled with green chemical engineering. However, industrial development still faces numerous challenges requiring concerted efforts from researchers in different fields.

passages.text: Inorganic pyrophosphate plasma levels in patients with GGCX-associated PXE-like phenotypes.

Introduction: Pseudoxanthoma elasticum (PXE) is an autosomal recessive ectopic calcification disorder clinically affecting the skin, eyes, and vascular system. Most cases of PXE are caused by inactivating pathogenic variants in the ABCC6 gene encoding a hepatic transmembrane efflux transporter, which facilitates the extracellular release of ATP, the precursor of inorganic pyrophosphate (PPi), a potent endogenous inhibitor of calcification. Pathogenic variants in GGCX, encoding gamma-glutamyl carboxylase required for activation of vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors as well as matrix Gla protein (MGP) and Gla-rich protein (GRP), two inhibitors of ectopic calcification, have also been reported to cause cutaneous changes like those seen in PXE. While ectopic calcification in ABCC6 deficiency has been associated with reduced plasma levels of PPi due to loss of ABCC6 transport activity in the liver, plasma PPi levels have not been reported in patients with GGCX-associated phenotypes. Methods: We analyzed five patients from three unrelated families on their clinical, laboratory, and molecular findings who carry biallelic variants in GGCX and present with phenotypic characteristics associated with PXE. The variants were identified using a next-generation sequencing panel consisting of 29 genes associated with ectopic calcification. Results and conclusion: This study demonstrates that in addition to ABCC6, GGCX variants can cause the PXE phenotype, expanding PXE and perhaps other heritable ectopic calcification disorders' clinical and genetic heterogeneity. The results also show that the plasma concentrations of PPi in these patients are not reduced compared to healthy control individuals, suggesting that plasma PPi does not govern ectopic calcification in GGCX deficiency.

passages.text: Protection of Broiler Chickens Against Necrotic Enteritis by Intrapulmonary Delivery of a Live Clostridium perfringens Vaccine Exploiting the Gut-Lung-Axis Concept.

Clostridium perfringens (CP)-induced necrotic enteritis (NE) is an economically important disease in the broiler chicken industry. The incidence of NE is common in 3-to-6-wk-old broiler chickens, once maternal antibodies start declining. Developing an effective vaccination strategy against NE, preferably delivering a single dose of vaccine at hatch to protect broiler chickens against NE without a booster vaccine, is an enormous challenge. The objective of this study was to induce mucosal immunity in the intestines against NE by intrapulmonary (IPL) delivery of a live CP vaccine at hatch, exploiting the gut-lung-axis (GLA) concept by vaccine delivery following in ovo administration of cytosine-phosphorothioate-guanine oligodeoxynucleotides (CpG-ODN) to induce immune cell maturation in the lungs. Experiments were conducted to explore the dose of CP and immune protection against heterologous CP challenge, and to study the efficacy of IPL delivery of a CP vaccine without a booster. Additional studies were conducted to measure serum immunoglobulin (Ig)Y, mucosal IgA, and histopathology of lungs following vaccination. Delivery of a live CP vaccine by the IPL route, with or without in ovo CpG-ODN, provided significant protection against NE (P < 0.0001). Systemic IgY and mucosal IgA against CP were correlated with protection against NE. There was no necrosis or inflammation in the pulmonary parenchyma. There was a low number of CP isolated from the lungs following live CP delivery by the IPL route. A significant influx of (P < 0.001) of CD8+ T cells and macrophages were noted in the lungs 2 days following live CP delivery by the IPL route. IPL delivery of a live CP vaccine, rather than inactivated CP, provided better protection. This study demonstrated the utility in exploiting the GLA concept in vaccine delivery in broiler chickens.

passages.text: Encapsulation nanoarchitectonics of glabridin with sophorolipid micelles for addressing biofilm hazards via extracellular polymeric substance permeation and srtA gene suppression.

BACKGROUND: Biofilm, a common drug-resistant phenotype of Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus), demonstrates significant drug resistance and recurrence due to its extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) barrier and subsequent bacterial migration. Hence, there is an urgent need for effective solutions to mitigate the hazards posed by biofilms. RESULT: This study developed a stable, low-toxicity multifunctional nanomicelle, GLA@SOL/EYL, by encapsulating glabridin (GLA) using sophorolipid (SOL) and egg yolk lecithin (EYL). Optimizations were performed for the hydration medium, the ratio of carrier materials to GLA, and EYL additions. GLA@SOL/EYL exhibited a particle size of 122.1 +- 0.8 nm and a surface potential of -66.4 +- 1.7 mV, endowing it with the ability to permeate biofilms EPS effectively. GLA@SOL/EYL encapsulated 98.3 +- 1.2 % of GLA and demonstrated a slow-release effect, significantly enhancing the bioavailability of GLA. The addition of EYL reduced the hemolytic toxicity of GLA@SOL/EYL and improved its encapsulation rate and stability. GLA@SOL/EYL reduced the minimum inhibitory concentration of GLA to 8 mug/mL and extended its inhibitory effect at low concentrations by rapidly disrupting the structural integrity of S. aureus. GLA@SOL/EYL may penetrate biofilms to disperse EPS and remove twice as much biofilm as GLA alone, thereby eliminating 99.99 % of S. aureus within biofilms, compared to 99 % bactericidal efficacy of GLA. Additionally, GLA@SOL/EYL inhibited 63.8 +- 1.8 % of biofilm formation by affecting the expression of the srtA gene, thereby reducing the expression of cell wall-anchoring protein genes. In contrast, the biofilm inhibition rates of GLA and blank micelles were less than 10 %. CONCLUSION: GLA@SOL/EYL utilizes the nanoparticle effect to penetrate biofilms and deliver antimicrobial GLA. The SOL disperses the biofilm matrix while GLA is released to kill S. aureus, preventing bacterial dissemination and colonization. Thus, GLA@SOL/EYL presents an innovative strategy for effectively eradicating S. aureus biofilms and preventing new hazards in a one-step approach.

passages.text: Safety Profiles Related to Dosing Errors of Rapid-Acting Insulin Analogs: A Comparative Analysis Using the EudraVigilance Database.

Insulin is essential for treating type 1 diabetes and insulin-requiring type 2 diabetes. BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Diabetes is a widespread condition that can lead to multiple and severe complications. Rapid-acting insulin analogs (RAIAs) and long-acting insulin analogs are prescribed for the effective management of diabetes. RAIAs are expected to be associated with a higher number of dosing errors because of their rapid onset, short duration of action, and the need for frequent dosing, compared to other insulin analogs. There are three approved RAIAs on the market: insulin lispro (LIS), insulin aspart (ASP), and insulin glulisine (GLU). The aim of this study is to evaluate the real-world evidence on dosing errors reported for RAIAs in EudraVigilance (EV), an established pharmacovigilance database, in comparison to other insulin analogs and human insulins. METHODS: A descriptive analysis and a disproportionality analysis were conducted. RESULTS: ASP and LIS were associated with high percentages of adverse drug reactions (ADRs) (22% and 17%, respectively), with over 70% of the reports involving serious ADRs. A higher frequency of cardiac and eye disorder ADRs was observed for LIS compared with ASP and GLU. GLU showed a higher frequency of ADRs in the skin and subcutaneous tissue disorders category. LIS dosing errors accounted for 5% of the total number of cases, while dosing errors for ASP and GLU were less than 3%. The most frequently reported dosing errors involved improper dosing (49%). CONCLUSIONS: Although there were fewer dosing errors of RAIAs in comparison to other insulins, the severity of the potential outcome highlights the importance of precise dosing and timing. Improved the monitoring and reporting of these dosing errors could enhance diabetes patient care. Additionally, smart medical devices could improve therapeutic outcomes.

passages.text: Study of Different Parameters Affecting Production and Productivity of Polyunsaturated Fatty Acids (PUFAs) and gamma-Linolenic Acid (GLA) by Cunninghamella elegans Through Glycerol Conversion in Shake Flasks and Bioreactors.

Microbial cultures repurposing organic industrial residues for value-added metabolite production is pivotal for sustainable resource use. Highlighting polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), particularly gamma-linolenic acid (GLA), renowned for their nutritional and therapeutic value. Notably, Zygomycetes' filamentous fungi harbor abundant GLA-rich lipid content, furthering their relevance in this approach. In this study, the strain C. elegans NRRL Y-1392 was evaluated for its capability to metabolize glycerol and produce lipids rich in GLA under different culture conditions. Various carbon-to-nitrogen ratios (C/N = 11.0, 110.0, and 220.0 mol/mol) were tested in batch-flask cultivations. The highest GLA production of 224.0 mg/L (productivity equal to 2.0 mg/L/h) was observed under nitrogen excess conditions, while low nitrogen content promoted lipid accumulation (0.59 g of lipids per g of dry biomass) without yielding more PUFAs and GLA. After improving the C/N ratio at 18.3 mol/mol, even higher PUFA (600 mg/L) and GLA (243 mg/L) production values were recorded. GLA content increased when the fungus was cultivated at 12  C (15.5% w/w compared to 12.8% w/w at 28  C), but productivity values decreased significantly due to prolonged cultivation duration. An attempt to improve productivity by increasing the initial spore population did not yield the expected results. The successful scale-up of fungal cultivations is evidenced by achieving consistent results (compared to flask experiments under corresponding conditions) in both laboratory-scale (Working Volume-Vw = 1.8 L; C/N = 18.3 mol/mol) and semi-pilot-scale (Vw = 15.0 L; C/N = 110.0 mol/mol) bioreactor experiments. To the best of our knowledge, cultivation of the fungus Cunninghamella elegans in glycerol-based substrates, especially in 20 L bioreactor experiments, has never been previously reported in the international literature. The successful scale-up of the process in a semi-pilot-scale bioreactor illustrates the potential for industrializing the bioprocess.

passages.text: Comparative cytotoxicity and mitochondrial disruption in H9c2 cardiomyocytes induced by common pesticides.

infons.name: Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions
Attention Deficit and Disruptive Behavior Disorders

passages.text: Chronic exposure to pesticides is believed to be associated with various human diseases, including cardiovascular diseases. However, the mechanisms by which pesticides lead to cardiovascular diseases remain unclear. In our study, we selected the following commonly used pesticides as typical examples: the herbicides glyphosate (GLY) and glufosinate ammonium (GLA); the insecticides imidacloprid (IMI) and thiamethoxam (THM); and the fungicides pyraclostrobin (PYR) and azoxystrobin (AZO). We employed H9c2 cells as a model to investigate the cytotoxic effects of these pesticides on myocardial cells at concentrations of 1, 10, 100, and 1000 mg/L. The results indicate that these pesticides can affect cell viability, alter the cell cycle, and significantly impact ATP content and mitochondrial complex levels, ultimately triggering oxidative stress responses in the cells. However, compared to herbicides GLY and GLA, insecticides IMI and THM, and fungicides PYR and AZO pesticides are more toxic to H9c2 cells. Additionally, GLY, GLA, IMI, THM, PYR, and AZO were found to cause structural changes in the mitochondria of H9c2 cells. Molecular docking results suggest that these pesticides can bind to proteins related to mitochondrial dynamics. Furthermore, IMI, THM, PYR, and AZO exhibit stronger binding abilities to mitochondrial dynamics-related proteins. These findings indicate that these pesticides significantly adverse effects on myocardial cells, mainly by causing mitochondrial dysfunction and inducing oxidative stress. Our findings highlight the importance of considering the differential toxicity of various classes of pesticides when assessing their risks to human health, particularly concerning cardiovascular diseases.

passages.text: An inducible model for medial calcification based on matrix Gla protein deficiency.

Calcific deposits in the arterial media have been associated with a number of metabolic and genetic disorders including diabetes, chronic kidney disease and generalized arterial calcification of infancy. The loss of Matrix Gla protein (MGP) leads to medial elastic lamina calcification (elastocalcinosis) in both humans and animal models. While MGP-deficient (Mgp-/-) mice have been used as a reliable model to study medial elastocalcinosis, these mice are difficult to maintain because of their fragility. Also, these mice are unsuitable for long-term calcification studies in relation to age and sex as most often they die prematurely. In order to circumvent these problems we generated Mgp-/-;ApoE-FGF23 mice, which in addition to the ablation of Mgp alleles, carries a transgene expressing the phosphaturic hormone FGF23. Increased FGF23 levels in the circulation and ensuing hypophosphatemia in these mice lead to a complete prevention of medial calcification until late adulthood. Interestingly, upon feeding a high phosphorus diet for 10 days, we were able to induce medial calcification in 3-week-old Mgp-/-;ApoE-FGF23 mice. Our mineral analyses showed that the calcific deposits in these mice were Our mineral analyses showed that the Ca/P % in the calcific deposits in these mice were comparable to that of 5-week-old Mgp-/- mice although the level of crystallinity differed. The aorta explants from Mgp-/-;ApoE-FGF23 mice resulted in elastocalcinosis in the presence of 2mM phosphate in the culture medium which was completely prevented by pyrophosphate analogue alendronate. Mgp-/-;ApoE-FGF23 mice will be suitable for future in vivo or ex vivo studies examining the effects of age, sex and mineralization inhibitors on medial elastocalcinosis.
